title: Host hardware must enable UEFI Secure Boot
description: UEFI Secure Boot is a security feature of the Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) specification. Its primary purpose is to ensure that only signed and trusted boot loaders and operating system kernels are allowed to execute during the system startup. The audit runs /usr/lib/vmware/secureboot/bin/secureBoot.py -s and expects "Enabled". Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 1.2 Host hardware must enable UEFI Secure Boot

audit.command:
out=$(/usr/lib/vmware/secureboot/bin/secureBoot.py -s 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
case "$out" in Enabled*) echo compliant ;; *) echo "secure boot: $out" ;; esac

remediation.command: You must enable the physical server's UEFI Secure Boot in the server BIOS/UEFI. 1. Put the non-compliant Host into maintenance mode: vim-cmd hostsvc/maintenance_mode_enter 2. Verify Secure Boot compatibility: /usr/lib/vmware/secureboot/bin/secureBoot.py -c 3. Restart the ESXi host with the reboot command. 4. on the ESXI physical host BIOS/UEFI configuration, ensure that "boot mode" is UEFI 5. Under Boot or Security menus, look for "Secure Boot" and set it to "Enabled". 6. Save all modified firmware changes and reboot the ESXi host. 7. Verify results.

title: Host image profile acceptance level must be PartnerSupported or higher
description: The acceptance level on ESXi regulates the type of software that can be installed on the system, with four distinct levels: VMwareCertified, VMwareAccepted, PartnerSupported, and CommunitySupported. It's advised to set the acceptance level to PartnerSupported or higher to ensure that only tested and digitally signed vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs) are allowed for ... The audit runs esxcli software acceptance get and accepts VMwareCertified, VMwareAccepted or PartnerSupported. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 2.4 Host image profile acceptance level must be PartnerSupported or higher

audit.command:
v=$(esxcli software acceptance get 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
case "$v" in VMwareCertified|VMwareAccepted|PartnerSupported) echo compliant ;; *) echo "acceptance level: $v" ;; esac

remediation.guidance: To verify the host image profile acceptance level perform the following: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure, then under System select Security Profile. 3. Under Host Image Profile Acceptance Level select Edit 4. In the dropdown select one of the following - VMware Certified, VMware Accepted, or Partner Supported. To implement the recommended configuration state, run the following PowerCLI command (in the example code, the level is Partner Supported): # Set the Software AcceptanceLevel for each host<span> Foreach ($VMHost in Get-VMHost ) { $ESXCli = Get-EsxCli -VMHost $VMHost $ESXCli.software.acceptance.Set("PartnerSupported") }

title: Host should deactivate SSH
description: Secure Shell (SSH) provides remote access to the ESXi shell, enabling direct host console access or remote connectivity. Deactivating SSH is a security measure aimed at minimizing remote access channels to the ESXi host, restricting it to essential connections only through vSphere Client, vCLI/PowerCLI, or published APIs. The audit parses vim-cmd hostsvc/hostconfig for the TSM-SSH service and requires startup policy "off" (start and stop manually) and the service not running. When tmaegis itself connects over SSH this rule reports the running service; scan from the ESXi Shell/DCUI instead. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.1 Host should deactivate SSH

audit.command:
out=$(vim-cmd hostsvc/hostconfig 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
p=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '/key = "TSM-SSH"/{f=1} f && $1=="policy" {v=$3; gsub(/[",]/, "", v); print v; exit}')
r=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '/key = "TSM-SSH"/{f=1} f && $1=="running" {v=$3; gsub(/[",]/, "", v); print v; exit}')
[ -n "$p" ] || { echo 'TSM-SSH: service not found in hostconfig'; exit 1; }
if [ "$p" = off ] && [ "$r" != true ]; then echo compliant; else echo "TSM-SSH: policy=$p running=$r"; fi

remediation.guidance: To disable SSH, perform the following: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Select Configure then expand System and select Services. 3. Click on SSH then click Edit Startup Policy. 4. Set the Startup Policy is set to Start and Stop Manually. 5. Click OK. 6. While ESXi Shell is still selected click Stop. Alternately, use the following PowerCLI command: # Set SSH to start manually rather than automatically for all hosts Get-VMHost | Get-VMHostService | Where { $_.key -eq "TSM-SSH" } | Set- VMHostService -Policy Off

title: Host must deactivate the ESXi shell
description: The ESXi shell is an interactive command line environment available from the Direct Console User Interface (DCUI) or remotely via SSH. Activities performed from the ESXi Shell bypass all access controls, but are logged. The recommended setting for the ESXi shell is to be stopped and only started manually when needed, such as when running diagnostics or troubleshooting. The audit parses vim-cmd hostsvc/hostconfig for the TSM (ESXi Shell) service and requires startup policy "off" and the service not running. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.2 Host must deactivate the ESXi shell

audit.command:
out=$(vim-cmd hostsvc/hostconfig 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
p=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '/key = "TSM"/{f=1} f && $1=="policy" {v=$3; gsub(/[",]/, "", v); print v; exit}')
r=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '/key = "TSM"/{f=1} f && $1=="running" {v=$3; gsub(/[",]/, "", v); print v; exit}')
[ -n "$p" ] || { echo 'TSM: service not found in hostconfig'; exit 1; }
if [ "$p" = off ] && [ "$r" != true ]; then echo compliant; else echo "TSM: policy=$p running=$r"; fi

remediation.guidance: To disable the ESXi shell, perform the following: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Select Configure then expand System and select Services. 3. Click on ESXi Shell then click Edit Startup Policy. 4. Set the Startup Policy is set to Start and Stop Manually. 5. Click on OK. Alternately, use the following PowerCLI command: # Set the ESXi shell to start manually rather than automatically for all hosts Get-VMHost | Get-VMHostService | Where { $_.key -eq "TSM" } | Set-VMHostService - Policy Off

title: Host must deactivate the ESXi Managed Object Browser (MOB)
description: The Managed Object Browser (MOB) is a web-based server application that lets you examine and change system objects and configurations. It is a prudent security measure to deactivate the MOB unless it's essential for operations. The parameter governing this behavior is Config.HostAgent.plugins.solo.enableMob with a recommended setting of False. The audit reads Config.HostAgent.plugins.solo.enableMob with esxcli and requires false (0). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.3 Host must deactivate the ESXi Managed Object Browser (MOB)

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Config/HostAgent/plugins/solo/enableMob 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/Config/HostAgent/plugins/solo/enableMob: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -eq 0 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Config/HostAgent/plugins/solo/enableMob = $v (expected false/0)"; fi

remediation.guidance: To disabled MOB, perform the following from the vSphere Web Client: 1. Select a host 2. Click Configure then expand System then select Advanced System Settings. 3. Click Edit then search for Config.HostAgent.plugins.solo.enableMob 4. Set the value to false. 5. Click OK. Note: You cannot disable the MOB while a host is in lockdown mode. Note 2: You must disable MOB from the vSphere interface not via the vim-cmd command.

title: Host must enforce password complexity
description: The enforcement of password complexity is managed through the Security.PasswordQualityControl parameter, allowing configuration of password length, character set requirements, and failed logon attempt restrictions. The recommended setting is "retry=3 min=disabled,15,15,15,15 max=64 similar=deny passphrase=3". The audit reads Security.PasswordQualityControl with esxcli and requires min=disabled,disabled,disabled,disabled,N with N of 15 or more. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.11 Host must enforce password complexity

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Security/PasswordQualityControl 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/^ *String Value: *//p' | head -n 1)
m=$(printf '%s\n' "$v" | tr ' ' '\n' | sed -n 's/^min=//p' | head -n 1)
[ -n "$m" ] || { echo "no min= in '$v'"; exit 1; }
printf '%s\n' "$m" | awk -F, '{ if (NF == 5 && $1 == "disabled" && $2 == "disabled" && $3 == "disabled" && $4 == "disabled" && $5 ~ /^[0-9]+$/ && $5 + 0 >= 15) print "compliant"; else print "min=" $0 }'

remediation.guidance: To set the password complexity requirements, perform the following PowerCLI command: Get-VMHOST | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name "Security.PasswordQualityControl" | Set- AdvancedSetting -Value "retry=3 min=disabled,disabled,disabled,disabled,15" The above requires all passwords to be 15 or more characters long and comprised of at least one character from four distinct character sets.

title: Host must enable lockdown mode
description: Implementing lockdown mode restricts direct access to ESXi hosts, mandating management via vCenter Server to uphold defined roles and access controls, mitigating risks associated with unauthorized or insufficiently audited activities. Exception Users list serves as an override mechanism, permitting specified users direct access even in lockdown mode. The audit runs vim-cmd -U dcui vimsvc/auth/lockdown_mode and requires lockdownNormal or lockdownStrict. Running the shell during lockdown requires the scanning account on the Exception Users list. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.20 Host must enable lockdown mode

audit.command:
out=$(vim-cmd -U dcui vimsvc/auth/lockdown_mode 2>/dev/null) || out=$(vim-cmd -U dcui vimsvc/auth/lockdown_is_enabled 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
case "$out" in *lockdownNormal*|*lockdownStrict*|true) echo compliant ;; *) echo "lockdown: $out" ;; esac

remediation.command: To enable lockdown mode, perform the following from the vSphere web client: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Select Configure then expand System and select Security Profile. 3. Across from Lockdown Mode click on Edit. 4. Click the radio button for Normal or Strict. 5. Click OK. Alternately, run the following PowerCLI command: # Enable lockdown mode for each host Get-VMHost | Foreach { $_.EnterLockdownMode() }

title: Host firewall must only allow traffic from authorized networks
description: The host's firewall is designed to block all incoming and outgoing network traffic by default, unless exceptions are explicitly made, thus minimizing the attack surface and barring unauthorized access. The firewall settings, while simplistic, are akin to router ACLs, and might require reflexive rules to be configured for certain network scenarios. The audit lists enabled firewall rulesets (esxcli network firewall ruleset list) and fails any whose allowed IP list (ruleset allowedip list) is All; confirm the configured ranges are the authorized networks. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.1 Host firewall must only allow traffic from authorized networks

audit.command:
en=$(esxcli network firewall ruleset list 2>/dev/null | awk 'NR > 2 && $2 == "true" {print $1}') || exit 1
all=$(esxcli network firewall ruleset allowedip list 2>/dev/null | awk 'NR > 2 && $2 == "All" {print $1}') || exit 1
bad=''
for r in $en; do for a in $all; do [ "$r" = "$a" ] && bad="$bad $r"; done; done
[ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || echo "enabled rulesets allowing all IPs:$bad"

remediation.command: To properly restrict access to services running on an ESXi host, perform the following from the vSphere web client: 1. Select a host 2. Click Configure then expand System then select Firewall. 3. Click Edit to view services which are enabled (indicated by a check). 4. For each enabled service, (e.g., ssh, vSphere Web Access, http client) provide a list of allowed IP addresses. 5. Click OK.

title: Host hardware must have auditable, authentic, and up to date system & device firmware
description: Hardware firmware is not immune to serious issues affecting confidentiality, integrity, or availability. Vulnerable system management controllers & management engines can provide places for attackers to establish persistence, in order to re-infect and re- compromise hosts after reboots and updates. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 1.1 Host hardware must have auditable, authentic, and up to date system & device firmware

audit.command: The preferred approach is to utilize a vendor-supported, VMware-compatible firmware and driver combination. Leverage Broadcom's Lifecycle Manager hardware compatibility checks or similar tools if available. If that is not available, manually inventory: System BIOS/UEFI BMC / iDRAC / iLO firmware TPM firmware RAID/storage controller firmware HBA firmware NIC firmware Fibre Channel adapter firmware NVMe / storage-device firmware where applicable GPU firmware where applicable compare those results with the currently supported and recommended baseline as well as VMware Compatibility Guide for ...

remediation.command: Proposed remediation guidelines: 1. Verify the exact server model and hardware components. 2. Obtain firmware only from the OEM/vendor: Dell HPE Lenovo Cisco etc. 3. Verify that the proposed firmware and associated ESXi driver are supported for your ESXi 8 release. 4. Place the ESXi host in maintenance mode. 5. Apply firmware through the vendor-supported mechanism (for example): Dell iDRAC / OpenManage HPE iLO / SPP Lenovo XClarity Cisco UCS Manager Vendor bootable firmware package Vendor Hardware Support Manager 6. Reboot the physical host if required. 7. Re-run the firmware inventory. 8. Confirm device/driver/firmware compatibility. 9. Exit maintenance mode.

title: Host hardware must enable Intel TXT, if available
description: Intel Xeon Scalable Processor platforms have Trusted Execution Technology, or TXT, that help harden systems against malware, rootkits, BIOS & firmware attacks, and more. When enabled, ESXi will take advantage of security benefits offered by this technology. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 1.3 Host hardware must enable Intel TXT, if available

audit.command: 1. Execute: esxcli hardware trustedboot get 2. For hardware that supports Intel Trusted Execution Technology, verify: Drtm Enabled: true Tpm Present: true Note: If Drtm Enabled is false, determine whether Intel TXT is supported by the host hardware and firmware. If TXT is supported but not enabled, the host is not compliant.

remediation.command: Place the ESXi host into maintenance mode and reboot the physical server. Enter the system BIOS/UEFI configuration and enable TPM 2.0 and Intel Trusted Execution Technology (TXT), where supported. Save the firmware configuration and perform a full reboot.

title: Host hardware must enable and configure a TPM 2.0
description: ESXi can use Trusted Platform Modules (TPM) 2.0 to enable advanced security features that prevent malware, remove dependencies, and secure hardware lifecycle operations. The audit runs esxcli hardware trustedboot get and requires "Tpm Present: true"; TPM attestation alarms are still reviewed in vCenter. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 1.4 Host hardware must enable and configure a TPM 2.0

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli hardware trustedboot get 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk -F': *' 'tolower($1) ~ /^ *tpm present$/ {print $2; exit}' | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | sed 's/ *$//')
if [ "$v" = true ]; then echo compliant; else echo "Tpm Present: ${v:-not reported}"; fi

remediation.command: 1. Place the host in maintenance mode. 2. reboot into BIOS/UEFI. 3. Enable and activate the TPM 4. Select TPM 2.0 mode, and ensure UEFI/Secure Boot prerequisites required by the server vendor are enabled. 5. Save changes. 6. reboot with command reboot 7. Verify again with esxcli hardware trustedboot get and esxcli system settings encryption get.

title: Host integrated hardware management controller must be secure
description: Many servers have integrated hardware management controllers that can be extremely helpful when monitoring and updating hardware, settings, and firmware. These controllers should be checked to ensure that ALL unused functionality is disabled, ALL unused access methods are disabled, passwords and password controls are set, and firewalling and access control is in place so that ... Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 1.5 Host integrated hardware management controller must be secure

audit.command: 1. Verify whether the ESXi host exposes a BMC interface: esxcli hardware ipmi bmc get 2. Find the hardware management controller and review: ; Firmware is current and vendor-supported. ; Default accounts and default passwords are not in use. ; Administrative accounts are individually assigned. ; Strong password/authentication policy is configured. ; MFA is enabled where supported. ; HTTPS/TLS is used for web management. ; Weak or obsolete protocols are disabled. ; SSH/IPMI access is disabled unless operationally required. ; Management access is restricted to authorized management networks.

remediation.command: Configure the controller according to the organization's secure-management baseline.

title: Host integrated hardware management controller must enable time synchronization
description: Cryptography, audit logging, cluster operations, and incident response/forensics depend deeply on synchronized time. This recommendation extends to all devices in infrastructure. The recommendation for NTP is to have at least four sources. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 1.6 Host integrated hardware management controller must enable time synchronization

audit.command: 1. Verify that NTP or another approved time synchronization mechanism is enabled 2. Verify that the ESXi host uses reliable time synchronization esxcli system ntp get

remediation.command: 1. Enable NTP or the vendor-supported automatic time synchronization service. 2. Enter the organization's approved NTP servers. 3. Configure multiple authoritative NTP sources where supported. 4. Configure the appropriate time zone. 5. Save/apply the configuration.

title: Host integrated hardware management controller must enable remote logging of events
description: The host's integrated hardware management controller provides critical out-of-band server oversight. For enhanced security, it is essential to configure this controller to log events remotely. This practice ensures that hardware-related logs are sent to an off-site location, protecting them from potential tampering and offering a centralized record of server health and ... Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 1.7 Host integrated hardware management controller must enable remote logging of events

audit.command: Access the hardware management controller and verify that remote event logging/syslog forwarding is enabled and configured to send hardware, security, authentication, and management events to an approved centralized log collector.

remediation.command: Locate the controller's Syslog, Remote Logging, Event Forwarding, or equivalent configuration and: 1. Enable remote event logging. 2. Configure the hostname or IP address of the approved centralized log collector. 3. Configure the appropriate port and protocol. 4. Use TLS or another protected transport where supported. 5. Select the required event categories, including hardware, security, authentication, firmware, and administrative events. 6. Save the configuration.

title: Host must run software that has not reached End of General Support status
description: The "End of General Support" (EOGS) status indicates that the software version has exceeded its primary support lifecycle, during which VMware provides new security patches, bug fixes, and technical assistance. When a product reaches this status, VMware no longer releases security updates for that version for customers outside of an extended support contract. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 2.1 Host must run software that has not reached End of General Support status

audit.command: 1. Execute vmware -vl or esxcli system version get 2. Record the ESXi version/build. 3. Compare the installed release to Broadcom's current lifecycle/support matrix. The host is compliant only when the installed ESXi release remains within General Support.

remediation.command: To remediate this recommendation, upgrade the host to an ESXi release/build that is still within Broadcom General Support. Use vSphere Lifecycle Manager or the vendor- supported image, validate hardware compatibility first, place the host in maintenance mode, remediate/upgrade, reboot, and verify the new build.

title: Host must have all software updates installed
description: Applying updates in a timely manner according to the severity of issues contributes greatly to the resilience of an environment. When applying updates, it is recommended to update vCenter Server first, if an update is available, and then proceed with updating ESXi. This sequence ensures that the management layer is updated before updating the ESXi hosts. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 2.2 Host must have all software updates installed

audit.command: Verify that the patches are up to date. The following PowerCLI snippet will provide a list of all installed patches: Foreach ($VMHost in Get-VMHost ) { $EsxCli = Get-EsxCli -VMHost $VMHost -V2 $EsxCli.software.vib.list.invoke() | Select-Object @{N="VMHost";E={$VMHost}},* } You may also manage updates via VMware Lifecycle Manager located under Menu, Lifecycle Manager.

remediation.command: Use VMware Lifecycle Manager to update and upgrade hosts when ESXi is managed through VMware vCenter. For standalone hosts use esxcli or API-driven methods for applying updates. Employ a process to keep ESXi hosts up to date with patches in accordance with industry standards and internal guidelines. Leverage the VMware Lifecycle Manager to test and apply patches as they become available.

title: Host must enable Secure Boot enforcement
description: Enabling Secure Boot enforcement ensures that the host only loads UEFI drivers and applications with valid digital signatures, as part of the UEFI firmware standard. It requires support from the server's BIOS and hypervisor boot loader, and mandates that all ESXi kernel modules, drivers, and VIBs be signed by VMware or a trusted partner subordinate. The audit runs esxcli system settings encryption get and requires "Require Secure Boot: true". Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 2.3 Host must enable Secure Boot enforcement

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings encryption get 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk -F': *' 'tolower($1) ~ /^ *require secure boot$/ {print $2; exit}' | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | sed 's/ *$//')
if [ "$v" = true ]; then echo compliant; else echo "Require Secure Boot: ${v:-not reported}"; fi

remediation.command: 1. Enable UEFI Secure Boot and TPM 2.0 on the hardware. 2. Configure ESXi secure configuration/Secure Boot enforcement using the supported vSphere/ESXCLI procedure for the installed ESXi 8 build. 3. Reboot if required and verify both secureBoot.py -s and esxcli system settings encryption get

title: Host must only run binaries delivered via signed VIB
description: The ESXi host is configured to only execute binaries originating from a valid, signed vSphere Installable Bundle (VIB) to enhance the integrity of the system. This measure thwarts attackers' attempts to use prebuilt toolkits on the host. The parameter governing this behavior is VMkernel.Boot.execInstalledOnly with a recommended setting of True. The audit runs esxcli system settings kernel list -o execInstalledOnly and requires the configured and runtime values to be TRUE. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 2.5 Host must only run binaries delivered via signed VIB

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings kernel list -o execInstalledOnly 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
set -- $(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="execInstalledOnly" {print toupper($3), toupper($4); exit}')
[ $# -eq 0 ] && { echo 'execInstalledOnly not listed'; exit 1; }
[ "$1" = TRUE ] && [ "$2" = TRUE ] && echo compliant || echo "execInstalledOnly configured=$1 runtime=$2"

remediation.guidance: 1. Remove unauthorized VIBs and set the kernel option with esxcli system settings kernel set -s execInstalledOnly -v TRUE 2. Reboot if the command or build indicates a reboot is required 3. Re-run the audit command and confirm only approved signed VIB-delivered binaries are executable.

title: Host must have reliable time synchronization sources
description: Ensuring reliable time synchronization is crucial as various functions like cryptography, audit logging, cluster operations, and incident response/forensics are heavily dependent on synchronized time. Utilizing at least four NTP sources is recommended for achieving reliable time synchronization. The audit runs esxcli system ntp get and requires NTP to be enabled with at least one server. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 2.6 Host must have reliable time synchronization sources

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system ntp get 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
en=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/^ *Enabled: *//p' | head -n 1)
srv=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/^ *Servers\{0,1\}: *//p' | head -n 1)
[ "$en" = true ] && [ -n "$srv" ] && echo compliant || echo "ntp enabled=$en servers=$srv"

remediation.command: To enable and properly configure NTP synchronization, perform the following from the vSphere web client: 1. Select a host 2. Click Configure then expand System then select Time Configuration. 3. Select Edit next to Network Time Protocol 4. Select the Enable box, then fill in the appropriate NTP Servers. 5. in the NTP Service Startup Policy drop down select Start and stop with host. 6. Click OK.

title: Host must have time synchronization services enabled and running
description: Ensure the host has time synchronization services enabled and operational as many functions such as cryptography, audit logging, cluster operations, and incident response/forensics depend on synchronized time. Services like NTP or PTP should be configured to start with the host and remain running to maintain time synchronization. The audit requires NTP enabled with servers (esxcli system ntp get) and the ntpd service running (/etc/init.d/ntpd status). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 2.7 Host must have time synchronization services enabled and running

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system ntp get 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
en=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/^ *Enabled: *//p' | head -n 1)
srv=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/^ *Servers\{0,1\}: *//p' | head -n 1)
[ "$en" = true ] && [ -n "$srv" ] || { echo "ntp enabled=$en servers=$srv"; exit 1; }
st=$(/etc/init.d/ntpd status 2>&1)
case "$st" in *'not running'*) echo 'ntpd is not running' ;; *running*) echo compliant ;; *) echo "ntpd status: $st" ;; esac

remediation.command: 1. Configure approved NTP servers 2. Enable the NTP client firewall ruleset if required 3. Set the NTP service startup policy to start and stop with the host, and start the service. Example: esxcli system ntp set --enabled true after configuring approved servers. Verify synchronization after remediation.

title: Host must require TPM-based configuration encryption
description: The host should enforce TPM-based configuration encryption to secure its configuration files, notably within the /etc/ directory or other namespaces. From vSphere 7.0 Update 2 onwards, configuration files archived are encrypted, leveraging a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to "seal" the configuration to the host, thereby enhancing security against offline attacks. The audit runs esxcli system settings encryption get and requires "Mode: TPM". Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 2.8 Host must require TPM-based configuration encryption

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings encryption get 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk -F': *' 'tolower($1) ~ /^ *mode$/ {print $2; exit}' | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | sed 's/ *$//')
if [ "$v" = tpm ]; then echo compliant; else echo "Mode: ${v:-not reported}"; fi

remediation.command: 1. Ensure TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot are enabled. 2. Take a backup of the ESXi recovery key 3. Configure the host to use TPM-backed configuration encryption using the supported ESXi secure-configuration procedure. 4. Reboot if required with the reboot command 5. Re-run esxcli system settings encryption get

title: Host must not suppress warnings about unmitigated hyperthreading vulnerabilities
description: It is imperative to retain hyperthreading security warnings as they indicate unmitigated CPU vulnerabilities. The parameter governing this behavior is UserVars.SuppressHyperthreadWarning, with a recommended setting of 0. The audit reads UserVars.SuppressHyperthreadWarning with esxcli and requires 0. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 2.9 Host must not suppress warnings about unmitigated hyperthreading vulnerabilities

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /UserVars/SuppressHyperthreadWarning 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/UserVars/SuppressHyperthreadWarning: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -eq 0 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/UserVars/SuppressHyperthreadWarning = $v (expected 0)"; fi

remediation.guidance: 1. Utilize the administrative PowerCLI session: execute Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name UserVars.SuppressHyperthreadWarning | Set-AdvancedSetting - Value 0 -Confirm:$false

title: Host must restrict inter-VM transparent page sharing
description: Transparent Page Sharing (TPS) aids in optimizing memory usage among virtual machines but under certain circumstances can be exploited to access data on adjacent virtual machines unauthorizedly. By configuring the Mem.ShareForceSalting parameter, inter-VM TPS is restricted, enhancing isolation and security. The audit reads Mem.ShareForceSalting with esxcli and requires 2. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 2.10 Host must restrict inter-VM transparent page sharing

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Mem/ShareForceSalting 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/Mem/ShareForceSalting: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -eq 2 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Mem/ShareForceSalting = $v (expected 2)"; fi

remediation.guidance: From the vSphere Web Client: 1. Select a host 2. Click Configure then expand System then select Advanced System settings. 3. Click Edit then Filter for Mem.ShareForceSalting. 4. Set the value to 2. 5. Click OK. Additionally, the following PowerCLI command can be used: Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name Mem.ShareForceSalting | Set-AdvancedSetting -Value 2

title: Host must use sufficient entropy for cryptographic operations
description: Starting with vSphere 8.0, ESXi has enhanced its entropy implementation to align with FIPS 140-3 and EAL4 certifications, ensuring a robust foundation for cryptographic operations. Kernel boot options dictate the activation of entropy sources on an ESXi host. The parameter governing this behavior is disableHwrng = FALSE and entropySources = 0. The audit runs esxcli system settings kernel list -o disableHwrng and requires it to be absent or FALSE (configured and runtime). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 2.11 Host must use sufficient entropy for cryptographic operations

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings kernel list -o disableHwrng 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
set -- $(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="disableHwrng" {print toupper($3), toupper($4); exit}')
[ $# -eq 0 ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }
[ "$1" = FALSE ] && [ "$2" = FALSE ] && echo compliant || echo "disableHwrng configured=$1 runtime=$2"

remediation.guidance: 1. Set the kernel option with: esxcli system settings kernel set -s disableHwrng -v FALSE 2. Reboot if required by the host/build and verify the configured and runtime values are FALSE.

title: Host must deactivate SLP
description: The Service Location Protocol (SLP) is used for the discovery and selection of network services in local area networks, which simplifies configuration by allowing computers to find necessary services automatically. The practice of deactivating SLP when not in use aligns with the principle of minimizing the attack surface by shutting down non-essential services. The audit runs /etc/init.d/slpd status and requires "not running". Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.4 Host must deactivate SLP

audit.command:
st=$(/etc/init.d/slpd status 2>&1)
case "$st" in *'not running'*) echo compliant ;; *running*) echo 'slpd is running' ;; *) echo "slpd status: $st"; exit 1 ;; esac

remediation.guidance: 1. Stop SLP if running: /etc/init.d/slpd stop Note: Confirm no operational dependency requires SLP before disabling it.

title: Host must deactivate CIM
description: Deactivating the Common Information Model (CIM) service, when not in use, aligns with the principle of minimizing the attack surface by disabling non-essential services. This action helps in reducing the potential vectors of attack, thus bolstering the host's security posture. The audit runs esxcli system wbem get and requires "Enabled: false". Document an exception when CIM is required. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.5 Host must deactivate CIM

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system wbem get 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk -F': *' 'tolower($1) ~ /^ *enabled$/ {print $2; exit}' | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | sed 's/ *$//')
if [ "$v" = false ]; then echo compliant; else echo "WBEM Enabled: ${v:-not reported}"; fi

remediation.guidance: Prerequisite Confirm monitoring/storage integrations do not require CIM/WBEM. If not required: 1. Disable WBEM/CIM using: esxcli system wbem set --enable false

title: Host should deactivate SNMP
description: Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) facilitates the management of networked devices. Minimize attack surface by disabling non-essential services. The recommended setting is to have the SNMP service stopped unless required and configured securely. The audit runs esxcli system snmp get and requires "Enable: false". When SNMP is required, document the exception and apply 6.4.1. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.6 Host should deactivate SNMP

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system snmp get 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk -F': *' 'tolower($1) ~ /^ *enable$/ {print $2; exit}' | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | sed 's/ *$//')
if [ "$v" = false ]; then echo compliant; else echo "SNMP Enable: ${v:-not reported}"; fi

remediation.guidance: 1. Disable SNMP when not required with: esxcli system snmp set --enable false If SNMP is required, restrict targets/communities, prefer secure SNMP configurations supported by the environment, and limit the ESXi firewall ruleset to authorized management networks.

title: Host must automatically terminate idle DCUI sessions
description: By configuring a session timeout, unattended console sessions are automatically terminated, thereby reducing the potential security risks associated with lingering active sessions. The parameter governing this behavior is UserVars.DcuiTimeOut, with a recommended setting of 600 (10 minutes). The audit reads UserVars.DcuiTimeOut with esxcli and requires 600 seconds or less (0 disables the timeout and fails). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.7 Host must automatically terminate idle DCUI sessions

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /UserVars/DcuiTimeOut 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/UserVars/DcuiTimeOut: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -gt 0 ] && [ "$v" -le 600 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/UserVars/DcuiTimeOut = $v (expected 1-600)"; fi

remediation.guidance: To correct the DCUI timeout setting, perform the following steps: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure, then under System select Advanced System Settings. 3. Select Edit then enter UserVars.DcuiTimeOut in the filter. 4. Click in the box for the current value, then set the value to 600 seconds or less. Alternately, use the following PowerCLI command: Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name UserVars.DcuiTimeOut | Set-AdvancedSetting -Value 600

title: Host must automatically terminate idle shells
description: The host should be configured to automatically terminate idle shell sessions to prevent potential unauthorized access due to forgotten logouts. Setting a timeout for idle SSH connections ensures that any unattended sessions are closed, thereby reducing the security risk. The parameter governing this behavior is UserVars. The audit reads UserVars.ESXiShellInteractiveTimeOut with esxcli and requires 300 seconds or less (0 disables it and fails). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.8 Host must automatically terminate idle shells

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /UserVars/ESXiShellInteractiveTimeOut 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/UserVars/ESXiShellInteractiveTimeOut: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -gt 0 ] && [ "$v" -le 300 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/UserVars/ESXiShellInteractiveTimeOut = $v (expected 1-300)"; fi

remediation.guidance: To set the timeout to the desired value, perform the following from the vSphere web client: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure then expand System. 3. Select Advanced System Settings then click Edit. 4. Enter ESXiShellInteractiveTimeOut in the filter. 5. Set the value for this parameter is set to the appropriate value (300 seconds or less). 6. Click OK. Note: A value of 0 disables the ESXi ShellInteractiveTimeOut. Alternately, use the following PowerCLI command: # Set Remove UserVars.ESXiShellInteractiveTimeOut to 300 on all hosts Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name 'UserVars.ESXiShellInteractiveTimeOut' | Set-AdvancedSetting -Value "300"

title: Host must automatically deactivate shell services
description: Enabling the automatic deactivation of shell services minimizes the attack surface on the host. The time window for the ESXi Shell and SSH services' availability is defined by UserVars.ESXiShellTimeOut, after which these services are terminated. The recommended setting for this parameter is 3600. The audit reads UserVars.ESXiShellTimeOut with esxcli and requires 3600 seconds or less (0 disables it and fails). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.9 Host must automatically deactivate shell services

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /UserVars/ESXiShellTimeOut 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/UserVars/ESXiShellTimeOut: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -gt 0 ] && [ "$v" -le 3600 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/UserVars/ESXiShellTimeOut = $v (expected 1-3600)"; fi

remediation.guidance: To set the timeout to the desired value, perform the following from the vSphere web client: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure then expand System. 3. Select Advanced System Settings then click Edit. 4. Enter ESXiShellTimeOut in the filter. 5. Set the value for this parameter is set to 3600 (1 hour) or less 6. Click OK. Note: A value of 0 disables the ESXiShellTimeOut. Alternately, run the following PowerCLI command: # Set UserVars.ESXiShellTimeOut to 3600 on all hosts Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name 'UserVars.ESXiShellTimeOut' | Set- AdvancedSetting -Value "3600"

title: Host must not suppress warnings that the shell is enabled
description: Having warnings for enabled SSH or ESXi Shell provides insight into potential security risks. Disabling such warnings can mask ongoing attacks. The parameter governing this behavior is UserVars.SuppressShellWarning with a recommended value of 0. The audit reads UserVars.SuppressShellWarning with esxcli and requires 0. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.10 Host must not suppress warnings that the shell is enabled

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /UserVars/SuppressShellWarning 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/UserVars/SuppressShellWarning: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -eq 0 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/UserVars/SuppressShellWarning = $v (expected 0)"; fi

remediation.guidance: From an administrative PowerCLI session. 1. Execute Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name UserVars.SuppressShellWarning | Set-AdvancedSetting -Value 0 -Confirm:$false 2. Shell access should normally remain disabled; do not suppress the warning when it is enabled.

title: Host must lock an account after a specified number of failed login attempts
description: The security control involves restricting account access following a specified number of failed login attempts, acting as a deterrent against brute-force attacks. This control is applicable for SSH and vSphere Web Services SDK access, though not for the Direct Console Interface (DCUI) and the ESXi Shell. The audit reads Security.AccountLockFailures with esxcli and requires 5. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.12 Host must lock an account after a specified number of failed login attempts

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Security/AccountLockFailures 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/Security/AccountLockFailures: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -eq 5 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Security/AccountLockFailures = $v (expected 5)"; fi

remediation.guidance: To set the maximum failed login attempts correctly, perform the following steps: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure then expand System. 3. Select Advanced System Settings then click Edit. 4. Enter Security.AccountLockFailures in the filter. 5. Set the value for this parameter to 5. Alternately, use the following PowerCLI command: Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name Security.AccountLockFailures | Set- AdvancedSetting -Value 5

title: Host must unlock accounts after a specified timeout period
description: Ensuring that user accounts on the ESXi host are automatically unlocked after a specified period contributes to a balance between security and operational usability. This mechanism reactivates idle accounts promptly while mitigating potential unauthorized access risks. The audit reads Security.AccountUnlockTime with esxcli and requires 900 seconds. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.13 Host must unlock accounts after a specified timeout period

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Security/AccountUnlockTime 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/Security/AccountUnlockTime: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -eq 900 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Security/AccountUnlockTime = $v (expected 900)"; fi

remediation.guidance: To set the account lockout to 15 minutes, perform the following: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure then expand System. 3. Select Advanced System Settings then click Edit. 4. Enter Security.AccountUnlockTime in the filter. 5. Set the value for this parameter to 900. Alternately, use the following PowerCLI command: Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name Security.AccountUnlockTime | Set- AdvancedSetting -Value 900

title: Host must configure the password history setting to restrict the reuse of passwords
description: The goal is to inhibit the reuse of past passwords, acting as a deterrent against potential security breaches stemming from the exploitation of old, compromised credentials. This is achieved by configuring the Security.PasswordHistory parameter, which specifies the number of unique passwords a user must cycle through before a previous password can be reused. The audit reads Security.PasswordHistory with esxcli and requires 5. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.14 Host must configure the password history setting to restrict the reuse of passwords

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Security/PasswordHistory 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/Security/PasswordHistory: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -eq 5 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Security/PasswordHistory = $v (expected 5)"; fi

remediation.guidance: To set the password history 5, perform the following: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure then expand System. 3. Select Advanced System Settings then click Edit. 4. Enter Security.PasswordHistory in the filter. 5. Set the value for this parameter is set to 5. Alternately, the following PowerCLI command may be used: Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting Security.PasswordHistory | Set-AdvancedSetting - Value 5

title: Host must be configured with an appropriate maximum password age
description: Implementing a maximum password age, as determined by the Security.PasswordMaxDays parameter, is aligned with modern password policies outlined in NIST 800-63B Section 5.1.1.2, which argue against forced periodic password changes provided that passwords have sufficient complexity. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.15 Host must be configured with an appropriate maximum password age

audit.command: From an administrative PowerCLI session 1. Execute Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name Security.PasswordMaxDays 2. Verify that the value matches organizational policy or 99999 when periodic password rotation is not required by policy.

remediation.command: 1. Set the approved value with Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name Security.PasswordMaxDays | Set-AdvancedSetting -Value <approved_days> -Confirm:$false 2. Document any policy-driven value that differs from the benchmark baseline.

title: Host must configure a session timeout for the API
description: A designated timeout ensures that sessions are not left open indefinitely, thereby reducing the exposure window for potential security threats. The parameter governing this behavior is Config.HostAgent.vmacore.soap.sessionTimeout with a recommended setting of 30 seconds. The audit reads Config.HostAgent.vmacore.soap.sessionTimeout with esxcli and requires the recommended 30 or less (0 disables the timeout and fails). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.16 Host must configure a session timeout for the API

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Config/HostAgent/vmacore/soap/sessionTimeout 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/Config/HostAgent/vmacore/soap/sessionTimeout: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -gt 0 ] && [ "$v" -le 30 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Config/HostAgent/vmacore/soap/sessionTimeout = $v (expected 1-30)"; fi

remediation.guidance: 1. Set the approved timeout with: Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name Config.HostAgent.vmacore.soap.sessionTimeout | Set- AdvancedSetting -Value <seconds> -Confirm:$false 2. Validate administrative integrations after the change.

title: Host must automatically terminate idle host client sessions
description: Configuring the host to automatically terminate idle host client sessions helps mitigate security risks associated with unattended sessions, which could potentially be exploited. The recommended setting for this control is a timeout value of 900. The parameter governing this behavior is UserVars.HostClientSessionTimeout. The audit reads UserVars.HostClientSessionTimeout with esxcli and requires 900 seconds or less (0 = unlimited fails). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.17 Host must automatically terminate idle host client sessions

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /UserVars/HostClientSessionTimeout 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/UserVars/HostClientSessionTimeout: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -gt 0 ] && [ "$v" -le 900 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/UserVars/HostClientSessionTimeout = $v (expected 1-900)"; fi

remediation.guidance: 1. Set the approved idle timeout with Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name UserVars.HostClientSessionTimeout | Set-AdvancedSetting -Value <seconds> -Confirm:$false 2. Reconnect to the Host Client and confirm inactive sessions expire as expected.

title: Host must have an accurate DCUI.Access list
description: The DCUI.Access parameter in VMware ESXi is used to specify a list of users who are permitted to access the Direct Console User Interface (DCUI) of the ESXi host, especially when Lockdown Mode is enabled. This parameter helps in controlling and securing access to the ESXi host by allowing only authorized users to override Lockdown Mode and access the DCUI, particularly in ... Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.18 Host must have an accurate DCUI.Access list

audit.command: To verify a proper trusted users list is set for DCUI, perform the following from the vSphere web client: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure then expand System. 3. Select Advanced System Settings then click Edit. 4. Enter DCUI.Access in the filter. 5. Verify that the DCUI.Access attribute is set to a comma-separated list of the users who are allowed to override lockdown mode. Alternately, the following PowerCLI command may be used: Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name DCUI.Access

remediation.command: To set a trusted users list for DCUI, perform the following from the vSphere web client: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure then expand System. 3. Select Advanced System Settings then click Edit. 4. Enter DCUI.Access in the filter. 5. Set the DCUI.Access attribute is set to a comma-separated list of the users who are allowed to override lockdown mode.

title: Host must have an accurate Exception Users list
description: Establishing an accurate Exception Users list is essential for managing user privileges during lockdown mode. Users on this list retain their privileges, making it imperative to include only those necessary for direct host access like service accounts for third-party solutions. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.19 Host must have an accurate Exception Users list

audit.command: To verify the membership of the "Exception Users" list, perform the following in the vSphere Web Client: 1. Select the host. 2. Click on Configure then expand System and select Security Profile. 3. Under Lockdown Mode view and verify the list of Exception Users for accuracy.

remediation.command: To correct the membership of the Exception Users list, perform the following in the vSphere Web Client: 1. Select the host. 2. Click on Configure then expand System and select Security Profile. 3. Select Edit next to Lockdown Mode. 4. Click on Exception Users. 5. Add or delete users as appropriate. 6. Click OK.

title: Host must deny shell access for the dcui account
description: The dcui account, utilized for process isolation for the Direct Console User Interface (DCUI), possesses shell access which, when deactivated, minimizes the attack surface. This action is a proactive measure to enhance system security. The audit runs esxcli system account list and requires Shell Access false for dcui. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.22 Host must deny shell access for the dcui account

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system account list 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="dcui" {print tolower($NF); exit}')
case "$v" in false) echo compliant ;; '') echo 'dcui not listed (or no Shell Access column on this build)'; exit 1 ;; *) echo 'dcui shell access: '"$v" ;; esac

remediation.command: Configure the dcui service account to have no shell access using the supported ESXi account-management mechanism for the installed build, and verify that the account cannot establish an interactive shell. Note: It is advised not to manually edit /etc/passwd unless directed by Broadcom support.

title: Host must display a login banner for the DCUI and Host Client
description: Enabling a login banner on the Direct Console User Interface (DCUI) and the Host Client interfaces provides a mechanism to display legal notices or organizational announcements at login. The parameter governing this behavior is Annotations.WelcomeMessage, with the recommended value being a text string aligned with organizational or legal advisories. The audit reads Annotations.WelcomeMessage with esxcli and requires a non-empty banner; confirm the text matches the approved legal notice. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.24 Host must display a login banner for the DCUI and Host Client

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Annotations/WelcomeMessage 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/^ *String Value: *//p' | head -n 1)
if [ -n "$v" ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Annotations/WelcomeMessage = '$v' (empty banner)"; fi

remediation.command: Set the approved banner using Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name Annotations.WelcomeMessage | Set-AdvancedSetting -Value '<approved banner>' - Confirm:$false, or configure it in Host > Configure > System > Advanced System Settings. Verify it displays in DCUI/Host Client.

title: Host must display a login banner for SSH connections
description: ESXi facilitates the display of a login message, primarily aimed to deter unauthorized access and inform legitimate users regarding system usage obligations, particularly during SSH connections. The text for this display is defined by a specific parameter, which is advisable to be configured, especially when SSH is active, albeit it's recommended to keep SSH in a stopped state ... The audit reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config and requires a Banner directive pointing to a non-empty file. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.25 Host must display a login banner for SSH connections

audit.command:
f=/etc/ssh/sshd_config; [ -r "$f" ] || exit 1
b=$(awk 'tolower($1)=="banner" {print $2; exit}' "$f")
case "$b" in ''|none) echo 'no SSH Banner configured'; exit 1 ;; esac
[ -s "$b" ] && echo compliant || echo "banner file $b is missing or empty"

remediation.guidance: 1. Configure Banner /etc/issue in the SSH configuration and place the approved warning text in the referenced file. 2. Restart SSH only if it is authorized to be running; otherwise leave SSH disabled.

title: Host must enable the highest version of TLS supported
description: The host should be configured to operate using the highest version of TLS supported to ensure secure communications. ESXi 8, by default, comes with TLS 1.2 enabled, although re-enabling other protocols is possible if required. Employing the highest version of TLS aids in protecting against known vulnerabilities present in older versions. The audit reads UserVars.ESXiVPsDisabledProtocols with esxcli and requires sslv3, tlsv1 and tlsv1.1 to be listed. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.26 Host must enable the highest version of TLS supported

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /UserVars/ESXiVPsDisabledProtocols 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | sed -n 's/^ *String Value: *//p' | head -n 1)
if printf "%s" "$v" | tr "A-Z" "a-z" | tr -d " " | tr "," "
" | grep -qx sslv3 && printf "%s" "$v" | tr "A-Z" "a-z" | tr -d " " | tr "," "
" | grep -qx tlsv1 && printf "%s" "$v" | tr "A-Z" "a-z" | tr -d " " | tr "," "
" | grep -qx "tlsv1[.]1"; then echo compliant; else echo "/UserVars/ESXiVPsDisabledProtocols = '$v' (expected sslv3,tlsv1,tlsv1.1 disabled)"; fi

remediation.guidance: Disable unsupported/legacy protocol versions using Broadcom-supported TLS configuration procedures for ESXi 8 and dependent services. Test vCenter, backup, monitoring, and API integrations before broad deployment.

title: Host must configure a persistent log location for all locally stored system logs
description: Configure the Syslog.global.logDir parameter to specify a persistent directory for system logs, ensuring they are retained across reboots. This can be set to a directory on mounted NFS or VMFS volumes, other than the default which is an in-memory filesystem that retains only a single day's worth of logs. The audit runs esxcli system syslog config get and requires "Local Log Output Is Persistent: true". Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1 Host must configure a persistent log location for all locally stored system logs

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system syslog config get 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk -F': *' 'tolower($1) ~ /^ *local log output is persistent$/ {print $2; exit}' | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | sed 's/ *$//')
if [ "$v" = true ]; then echo compliant; else echo "Local Log Output Is Persistent: ${v:-not reported}"; fi

remediation.command: To configure persistent logging properly, perform the following from the vSphere web client: 1. Select the host 2. Click Configure then expand System then select Advanced System Settings. 3. Select Edit then enter Syslog.global.LogDir in the filter. 4. Set Syslog.global.logDir to a persistent location specified as [datastorename] path_to_file where the path is relative to the datastore. For example, [datastore1] /systemlogs. 5. Click OK. Alternatively, run the following PowerCLI command: # Set Syslog.global.logDir for each host Get-VMHost | Foreach { Set-AdvancedConfiguration -VMHost $_ -Name Syslog.global.logDir -Value "<NewLocation>" }

title: Host must transmit system logs to a remote log collector
description: Transmitting system logs to a remote log collector ensures that ESXi logs are stored in a secure and centralized manner. This centralization not only allows for the streamlined monitoring of all hosts through a single tool but also facilitates aggregate analysis and searching capabilities. The audit reads Syslog.global.logHost with esxcli and requires it to be set. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.2 Host must transmit system logs to a remote log collector

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Syslog/global/logHost 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/^ *String Value: *//p' | head -n 1)
[ -n "$v" ] && echo compliant || echo 'Syslog.global.logHost is empty'

remediation.command: To configure remote logging properly, perform the following from the vSphere web client: 1. Select the host 2. Click Configure then expand System then select Advanced System Settings. 3. Select Edit then enter Syslog.global.logHost in the filter. 4. Set the Syslog.global.logHost to the hostname or IP address of the central log server. 5. Click OK. Alternately, run the following PowerCLI command: # Set Syslog.global.logHost for each host Get-VMHost | Foreach { Set-AdvancedSetting -VMHost $_ -Name Syslog.global.logHost -Value "<NewLocation>" } Note: When setting a remote log host, it is also recommended to set the "Syslog.global.logDirUnique" to true.

title: Host must log sufficient information for events
description: Set the Syslog.global.logLevel parameter to "info" to ensure that audit logs capture sufficient information for diagnosing issues and investigating security events. This setting strikes a balance between log verbosity and storage utilization. The parameter governing this behavior is Syslog.global.logLevel with a recommended setting of info. The audit reads Syslog.global.logLevel with esxcli and requires info; also review logger rotation/size (esxcli system syslog config logger list). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.3 Host must log sufficient information for events

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Syslog/global/logLevel 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/^ *String Value: *//p' | head -n 1)
if [ "$v" = info ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Syslog/global/logLevel = '$v' (expected info)"; fi

remediation.guidance: 1. Increase the number of rotations and/or individual log size 2. esxcli system syslog config logger set --id=vmkernel -- rotate=15 --size=10240 3. esxcli system syslog config logger set --id=hostd -- rotate=15 --size=10240

title: Host must set the logging informational level to info
description: Set the logging informational level to "info" via the Config.HostAgent.log.level parameter to ensure audit logs contain adequate data for diagnostics and forensics. This level provides a balanced amount of detail, suitable for routine analysis and investigation. The parameter governing this behavior is Config.HostAgent.log.level with a recommended setting of info. The audit reads Config.HostAgent.log.level with esxcli and requires info. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.4 Host must set the logging informational level to info

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Config/HostAgent/log/level 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/^ *String Value: *//p' | head -n 1)
if [ "$v" = info ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Config/HostAgent/log/level = '$v' (expected info)"; fi

remediation.guidance: Using the vSphere client: Host → Configure → System → Advanced System Settings → Syslog.global.logLevel Set: info Execute command: esxcli system syslog config get | grep "Log Level" Verify - Log Level: info

title: Host must deactivate log filtering
description: Log filtering can be employed to diminish the frequency of repetitive log entries and to preclude specific log events entirely. By employing the Syslog.global.logFilters configuration parameter, one can stipulate filtering criteria, which when met, will cause the designated log events to be excluded from the system logs. The audit reads Syslog.global.logFiltersEnable with esxcli and requires false (0). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.5 Host must deactivate log filtering

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Syslog/global/logFiltersEnable 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/Syslog/global/logFiltersEnable: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -eq 0 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Syslog/global/logFiltersEnable = $v (expected false/0)"; fi

remediation.guidance: 1. Disable log filtering 2. execute command: esxcli system syslog config logfilter set -- log-filtering-enabled=false 3. execute: Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name "Syslog.global.logFiltersEnable" passing value is: False

title: Host must enable audit record logging
description: Enabling audit record logging on ESXi hosts ensures the local storage of audit records, providing a trail of activities performed on the host. This measure is pivotal for accountability, troubleshooting, and security investigations. The parameter governing this behavior is Syslog.global.auditRecord.storageEnable with a recommended setting of TRUE. The audit reads Syslog.global.auditRecord.storageEnable with esxcli and requires true (1). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.6 Host must enable audit record logging

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Syslog/global/auditRecord/storageEnable 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/Syslog/global/auditRecord/storageEnable: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -eq 1 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Syslog/global/auditRecord/storageEnable = $v (expected true/1)"; fi

remediation.guidance: To enable local audit-record logging: 1. Execute command: esxcli system auditrecords local enable 2. Verify remediation with: esxcli system auditrecords get 3. passing results: Audit Record Storage Active: true

title: Host must configure a persistent log location for all locally stored audit records
description: Configuring a persistent log location for locally stored audit records on ESXi hosts is critical to ensure audit continuity. When the "/scratch" directory is linked to "/tmp/scratch", only a day's worth of records are retained, and they are reinitialized upon each reboot, creating a security risk. The audit reads Syslog.global.auditRecord.storageDirectory with esxcli and requires a datastore path (/vmfs/volumes/... or [datastore] ...); the default /scratch location fails. Do not use a vSAN datastore. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.7 Host must configure a persistent log location for all locally stored audit records

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Syslog/global/auditRecord/storageDirectory 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/^ *String Value: *//p' | head -n 1)
if case "$v" in /vmfs/volumes/?*|\[*\]*) true ;; *) false ;; esac; then echo compliant; else echo "/Syslog/global/auditRecord/storageDirectory = '$v' (expected a persistent datastore path)"; fi

remediation.command: Configure a persistent datastore location with: esxcli system auditrecords local set \ -- directory=/vmfs/volumes/<Datastore-UUID>/audit/<hostname> then esxcli system auditrecords local enable verify compliance with: esxcli system auditrecords get compliant results = Audit Record Storage Active: true Audit Record Storage Directory: /vmfs/volumes/<Datastore-UUID>/audit/<hostname>

title: Host must store one week of audit records
description: Ensuring a local storage capacity for a week's worth of audit records is imperative, especially when a remote audit record storage facility is used. This provision is critical during anticipated interruptions in record delivery to the remote facility, preventing loss or overwriting of audit records. The audit reads Syslog.global.auditRecord.storageCapacity (MiB) with esxcli and requires the recommended 100 or more; confirm it holds 7 days of records. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.8 Host must store one week of audit records

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Syslog/global/auditRecord/storageCapacity 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/Syslog/global/auditRecord/storageCapacity: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -ge 100 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Syslog/global/auditRecord/storageCapacity = $v (expected 100 or more)"; fi

remediation.guidance: Increase the local audit-record storage capacity to store at least 7 days worth of audit logs. execute: esxcli system auditrecords local set --size=<MiB>

title: Host must transmit audit records to a remote log collector
description: This control enables the forwarding of audit records from the ESXi host to a designated log collector, aiding in real-time monitoring and analysis. The parameter governing this behavior is Syslog.global.auditRecord.remoteEnable with a recommended setting of TRUE. The audit requires Syslog.global.logHost to be set and Syslog.global.auditRecord.remoteEnable to be true (1). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.9 Host must transmit audit records to a remote log collector

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Syslog/global/logHost 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/^ *String Value: *//p' | head -n 1)
[ -n "$v" ] || { echo 'Syslog.global.logHost is empty'; exit 1; }
out2=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Syslog/global/auditRecord/remoteEnable 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out2" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/Syslog/global/auditRecord/remoteEnable: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -eq 1 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Syslog/global/auditRecord/remoteEnable = $v (expected true/1)"; fi

remediation.command: To configure remote logging properly, perform the following from the vSphere web client: 1. Select the host 2. Click Configure then expand System then select Advanced System Settings. 3. Select Edit then enter Syslog.global.logHost in the filter. 4. Set the Syslog.global.logHost to the hostname or IP address of the central log server. 5. Click OK. Alternately, run the following PowerCLI command: # Set Syslog.global.logHost for each host Get-VMHost | Foreach { Set-AdvancedSetting -VMHost $_ -Name Syslog.global.logHost -Value "<NewLocation>" } Note: When setting a remote log host, it is also recommended to set the "Syslog.global.logDirUnique" to true.

title: Host must verify certificates for TLS remote logging endpoints
description: When engaging in remote logging activities, it is of utmost importance to ensure that the logging endpoint is genuine and secure. To achieve this, hosts should verify the TLS certificates of these endpoints. This verification provides assurance that the endpoint is both authentic and trustworthy, mitigating the risk of transmitting logs to potentially malicious or untrusted ... The audit reads Syslog.global.certificate.checkSSLCerts with esxcli and requires true (1). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.10 Host must verify certificates for TLS remote logging endpoints

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Syslog/global/certificate/checkSSLCerts 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/Syslog/global/certificate/checkSSLCerts: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -eq 1 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Syslog/global/certificate/checkSSLCerts = $v (expected true/1)"; fi

remediation.guidance: Execute command: esxcli system syslog config set --check-ssl- certs=true Verify with: esxcli system syslog config get remediated result should include: ssl://

title: Host must use strict x509 verification for TLS-enabled remote logging endpoints
description: When employing remote logging with TLS-enabled endpoints, it is essential to ensure the utmost integrity and authenticity of the certificates in use. The "x509-strict" option provides a higher level of security by performing additional validity checks on CA root certificates during the verification process. The audit reads Syslog.global.certificate.strictX509Compliance with esxcli and requires true (1). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.11 Host must use strict x509 verification for TLS-enabled remote logging endpoints

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Syslog/global/certificate/strictX509Compliance 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/Syslog/global/certificate/strictX509Compliance: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -eq 1 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Syslog/global/certificate/strictX509Compliance = $v (expected true/1)"; fi

remediation.guidance: Utilize PowerCLI to remediate </> Powershell Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name "Syslog.global.certificate.strictX509Compliance" | Set-AdvancedSetting -Value $true -Confirm:$false Verify with Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name "Syslog.global.certificate.strictX509Compliance" Expected Calue is: Value = True

title: Host must block network traffic by default
description: By default, the host is configured to block all incoming and outgoing network traffic, except for the traffic pertaining to services enabled in the host security profile. This configuration is pivotal in reducing the attack surface and averting unauthorized access to the host. The audit runs esxcli network firewall get and requires "Enabled: true" and "Default Action: DROP"; review enabled rulesets as well. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.2 Host must block network traffic by default

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli network firewall get 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
a=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/^ *Default Action: *//p' | head -n 1)
e=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/^ *Enabled: *//p' | head -n 1)
[ "$a" = DROP ] && [ "$e" = true ] && echo compliant || echo "firewall enabled=$e default action=$a"

remediation.command: 1. Enable the ESXi firewall if disabled and disable unnecessary rulesets. 2. Use: esxcli network firewall set --enabled true 3. Configure only the required rulesets for documented services.

title: Host must restrict use of the dvFilter network API
description: The Net.DVFilterBindIpAddress parameter controls the use of the dvFilter network API, allowing network information to be sent to a specified IP address. If enabled with a compromised IP address, unauthorized network access to other virtual machines on the host could occur. It's essential to keep this parameter unconfigured, unless required by a product like VMware NSX. The audit reads Net.DVFilterBindIpAddress with esxcli and requires an empty value (set it only when a dvfilter security appliance is used). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.3 Host must restrict use of the dvFilter network API

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Net/DVFilterBindIpAddress 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/^ *String Value: *//p' | head -n 1)
if [ -z "$v" ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Net/DVFilterBindIpAddress = '$v' (expected empty)"; fi

remediation.guidance: To remove the configuration for the dvfilter network API, perform the following from the vSphere web client: 1. From the vSphere web client, select the host and click Configure then expand System 2. Click on Advanced System Settings then Edit. 3. Search for Net.DVFilterBindIpAddress in the filter. 4. Set Net.DVFilterBindIpAddress has an empty value. 5. If an appliance is being used, make sure the value of this parameter is set to the proper IP address. 6. Enter the proper IP address. 7. Click OK.

title: Host must filter Bridge Protocol Data Unit (BPDU) packets
description: To prevent cascading lockout of uplink interfaces from the ESXi host, the Net.BlockGuestBPDU parameter can be set to 1, enabling BPDU Filter to drop BPDU packets sent from virtual machines to the physical switch. This is crucial as ESXi's Standard and Distributed Virtual Switches do not support STP, making them prone to network loops if BPDUs are unfiltered. The audit reads Net.BlockGuestBPDU with esxcli and requires 1. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.4 Host must filter Bridge Protocol Data Unit (BPDU) packets

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Net/BlockGuestBPDU 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/Net/BlockGuestBPDU: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -eq 1 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Net/BlockGuestBPDU = $v (expected 1)"; fi

remediation.guidance: From an administrative PowerCLI session: Execute - Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name Net.BlockGuestBPDU | Set-AdvancedSetting - Value 1 -Confirm:$false. Validate network appliances/virtual switching workloads before enforcing this setting.

title: Host should reject forged transmits on standard virtual switches and port groups
