description: Setting the "Forged transmits" option to "Reject" helps prevent MAC impersonation by comparing the source MAC address from the guest operating system with the effective MAC address of its virtual machine adapter. If there's a mismatch, the packet is dropped, preventing potential malicious activities through impersonated MAC addresses. The audit runs esxcli network vswitch standard (portgroup) policy security get for every standard vSwitch and port group and requires "Allow Forged Transmits: false". Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.6 Host should reject forged transmits on standard virtual switches and port groups

audit.command:
command -v esxcli >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1
vs=$(esxcli network vswitch standard list 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^ *Name: *//p') || exit 1
pgs=$(esxcli --formatter=csv network vswitch standard portgroup list 2>/dev/null | awk -F, 'NR==1 {for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) if ($i == "Name") c = i; next} c {print $c}') || exit 1
out=$(for v in $vs; do
  x=$(esxcli network vswitch standard policy security get -v "$v" 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^ *Allow Forged Transmits: *//p' | head -n 1)
  [ "$x" = false ] || echo "vSwitch $v: Allow Forged Transmits=${x:-unknown}"
done
printf '%s\n' "$pgs" | while IFS= read -r p; do [ -n "$p" ] || continue
  x=$(esxcli network vswitch standard portgroup policy security get -p "$p" 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^ *Allow Forged Transmits: *//p' | head -n 1)
  [ "$x" = false ] || echo "portgroup $p: Allow Forged Transmits=${x:-unknown}"
done)
[ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out"

remediation.guidance: To set the policy to reject forged transmissions, perform the following: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure then expand Networking. 3. Select Virtual switches then click Edit. 4. Click on Security. 5. Set Forged transmits to Reject in the dropdown. 6. Click on OK. Alternately, the following ESXi shell command may be used: # esxcli network vswitch standard policy security set -v vSwitch2 -f false

title: Host should reject MAC address changes on standard virtual switches and port groups
description: Enforcing MAC address stability on standard virtual switches and port groups prevents MAC impersonation by disallowing changes to the MAC address by virtual machines. This mitigates the risk of malicious activities initiated by impersonating authorized network adapters. The audit runs esxcli network vswitch standard (portgroup) policy security get for every standard vSwitch and port group and requires "Allow MAC Address Change: false". Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.7 Host should reject MAC address changes on standard virtual switches and port groups

audit.command:
command -v esxcli >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1
vs=$(esxcli network vswitch standard list 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^ *Name: *//p') || exit 1
pgs=$(esxcli --formatter=csv network vswitch standard portgroup list 2>/dev/null | awk -F, 'NR==1 {for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) if ($i == "Name") c = i; next} c {print $c}') || exit 1
out=$(for v in $vs; do
  x=$(esxcli network vswitch standard policy security get -v "$v" 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^ *Allow MAC Address Change: *//p' | head -n 1)
  [ "$x" = false ] || echo "vSwitch $v: Allow MAC Address Change=${x:-unknown}"
done
printf '%s\n' "$pgs" | while IFS= read -r p; do [ -n "$p" ] || continue
  x=$(esxcli network vswitch standard portgroup policy security get -p "$p" 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^ *Allow MAC Address Change: *//p' | head -n 1)
  [ "$x" = false ] || echo "portgroup $p: Allow MAC Address Change=${x:-unknown}"
done)
[ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out"

remediation.guidance: To set the policy to reject, perform the following: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure then expand Networking. 3. Select Virtual switches then click Edit. 4. Click on Security. 5. Set MAC address changes to Reject in the dropdown. 6. Click on OK. Alternately, perform the following using the ESXi shell: # esxcli network vswitch standard policy security set -v vSwitch2 -m false

title: Host should reject promiscuous mode requests on standard virtual switches and port groups
description: Enabling promiscuous mode allows all virtual machines in a port group to read all packets transmitted across it, regardless of the intended recipient. Rejecting promiscuous mode requests on standard virtual switches and port groups prevents unauthorized packet inspection, enhancing network isolation and data privacy. The audit runs esxcli network vswitch standard (portgroup) policy security get for every standard vSwitch and port group and requires "Allow Promiscuous: false". Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.8 Host should reject promiscuous mode requests on standard virtual switches and port groups

audit.command:
command -v esxcli >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1
vs=$(esxcli network vswitch standard list 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^ *Name: *//p') || exit 1
pgs=$(esxcli --formatter=csv network vswitch standard portgroup list 2>/dev/null | awk -F, 'NR==1 {for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) if ($i == "Name") c = i; next} c {print $c}') || exit 1
out=$(for v in $vs; do
  x=$(esxcli network vswitch standard policy security get -v "$v" 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^ *Allow Promiscuous: *//p' | head -n 1)
  [ "$x" = false ] || echo "vSwitch $v: Allow Promiscuous=${x:-unknown}"
done
printf '%s\n' "$pgs" | while IFS= read -r p; do [ -n "$p" ] || continue
  x=$(esxcli network vswitch standard portgroup policy security get -p "$p" 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^ *Allow Promiscuous: *//p' | head -n 1)
  [ "$x" = false ] || echo "portgroup $p: Allow Promiscuous=${x:-unknown}"
done)
[ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out"

remediation.command: To set the policy to reject, perform the following: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure then expand Networking. 3. Select Virtual switches then click Edit. 4. Click on Security. 5. Set Promiscuous mode to Reject in the dropdown. 6. Click on OK. Alternately, perform the following via the ESXi shell: # esxcli network vswitch standard policy security set -v vSwitch2 -p false

title: Host must restrict access to a default or native VLAN on standard virtual switches
description: ESXi does not use the concept of native VLAN, so do not configure port groups to use the native VLAN ID. If the default value of 1 for the native VLAN is being used, the ESXi Server virtual switch port groups should be configured with any value between 2 and 4094. Otherwise, ensure that the port group is not configured to use whatever value is set for the native VLAN. The audit lists standard port groups (esxcli --formatter=csv network vswitch standard portgroup list) and fails any using VLAN ID 1, the usual default/native VLAN; adjust if your physical switches use another native VLAN. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.9 Host must restrict access to a default or native VLAN on standard virtual switches

remediation.command: To stop using the native VLAN ID for port groups, perform the following: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure then expand Networking. 3. Select Virtual switches. 4. Expand the Standard vSwitch. 5. View the topology diagram of the switch, which shows the various port groups associated with that switch. 6. For each port group on the vSwitch, verify and record the VLAN IDs used. 7. If a VLAN ID change is needed, click the name of the port group in the topology diagram of the virtual switch. 8. Click the Edit settings option. 9. In the Properties section, enter an appropriate name in the Network label field. 10. In the VLAN ID dropdown select or type a new VLAN.

title: Host must restrict the use of Virtual Guest Tagging (VGT) on standard virtual switches
description: When a port group is set to VLAN 4095 on standard virtual switches, it enables Virtual Guest Tagging (VGT), letting all network frames pass to the attached virtual machines (VMs) without altering the VLAN tags. This requires VMs to process VLAN information themselves via an 802.1Q driver. The audit lists standard port groups and fails any using VLAN ID 4095 (Virtual Guest Tagging); document the exception when VGT is required. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.10 Host must restrict the use of Virtual Guest Tagging (VGT) on standard virtual switches

remediation.command: To set port groups to values other than 4095 and 0 unless VGT is required, perform the following: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure then expand Networking. 3. Select Virtual switches. 4. Expand the Standard vSwitch. 5. View the topology diagram of the switch, which shows the various port groups associated with that switch. 6. For each port group on the vSwitch, verify and record the VLAN IDs used. 7. If a VLAN ID change is needed, click the name of the port group in the topology diagram of the virtual switch. 8. Click the Edit settings option. 9. In the Properties section, enter an appropriate name in the Network label field. 10.

title: Host must isolate management communications
description: Ensure that only vmk interfaces designated for management purposes have management services enabled to uphold network isolation and security. Incorrect configuration may undermine security efforts by breaching network isolation principles. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.11 Host must isolate management communications

audit.command: Review VMkernel adapters with: esxcli network ip interface list Verify that management traffic is carried only on dedicated, approved VMkernel interfaces/VLANs and is not mixed with untrusted VM, storage, vMotion, or public traffic without an approved design.

remediation.command: To remediate this recommendation, create or move management VMkernel interfaces to dedicated management port groups/VLANs, apply firewall/ACL restrictions, and remove management service flags from interfaces that do not require them. Test vCenter connectivity before deleting the old path.

title: Host CIM services, if enabled, must limit access
description: The Common Information Model (CIM) system allows for hardware-level management from remote applications through standard APIs. Ensuring only minimal access necessary to these applications is imperative to prevent potential security compromises. A dedicated service account, specific to each CIM application, should be created to limit access and privileges. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 6.1.1 Host CIM services, if enabled, must limit access

audit.command: To verify CIM access is limited, check for a limited-privileged service account with the following CIM roles applied: Host.Config.SystemManagement Host.CIM.CIMInteraction Alternately, the following PowerCLI command may be used: # List all user accounts on the Host -Host Local connection required- Get-VMHostAccount

remediation.command: To limit CIM access, perform the following: 1. Create a limited-privileged service account for CIM and other third-party applications. 2. This account should access the system via vCenter. 3. Give the account the CIM Interaction privilege only. This will enable the account to obtain a CIM ticket, which can then be used to perform both read and write CIM operations on the target host. If an account must connect to the host directly, this account must be granted the full "Administrator" role on the host. This is not recommended unless required by the monitoring software being used.

title: Host must isolate storage communications
description: Isolating storage communications through zoning and Logical Unit Number (LUN) masking is instrumental in segregating Storage Area Network (SAN) activity. Zoning defines the connections between host bus adapters (HBAs) and targets, ensuring devices outside a zone remain invisible to the devices within, thus facilitating the independent management of zones such as testing and ... Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 6.2.1 Host must isolate storage communications

audit.command: The audit procedures to verify SAN activity is properly segregated are SAN vendor or product-specific.

remediation.command: The remediation procedures to properly segregate SAN activity are SAN vendor or product-specific. In general, with ESXi hosts, use a single-initiator zoning or a single-initiator-single-target zoning. The latter is a preferred zoning practice. Using the more restrictive zoning prevents problems and misconfigurations that can occur on the SAN.

title: Host must ensure all datastores have unique names
description: Ensuring unique naming for datastores is crucial to avoid potential errors that could affect the integrity and availability of data. A descriptive and unique name for each datastore facilitates better identification and management. Although there's no specific parameter to enforce this, manual or automated naming conventions should be adhered to. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 6.2.2 Host must ensure all datastores have unique names

audit.command: List datastores with: esxcli storage filesystem list or PowerCLI Get-Datastore Verify that datastore names are unique across the managed vCenter inventory and are descriptive enough to prevent administrative ambiguity.

remediation.command: See the CIS benchmark remediation procedure.

title: Host iSCSI client, if enabled, must employ bidirectional/mutual CHAP authentication
description: Implementing bidirectional CHAP authentication for iSCSI connections elevates security by necessitating mutual verification between the initiator (client) and target (server), ensuring data integrity during transmission. Configuration involves setting the iSCSI storage adapter authentication to "Use bidirectional CHAP" and providing the requisite credentials. The audit lists iSCSI adapters (esxcli iscsi adapter list) and requires CHAP level "required" in both uni and mutual directions on each; with no iSCSI adapters the rule passes. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 6.3.1 Host iSCSI client, if enabled, must employ bidirectional/mutual CHAP authentication

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli iscsi adapter list 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
ad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk 'NR > 2 && $1 ~ /^vmhba/ {print $1}')
bad=''
for a in $ad; do
  u=$(esxcli iscsi adapter auth chap get -A "$a" -d uni 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^ *Level: *//p' | head -n 1)
  m=$(esxcli iscsi adapter auth chap get -A "$a" -d mutual 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^ *Level: *//p' | head -n 1)
  [ "$u" = required ] && [ "$m" = required ] || bad="$bad $a(uni=${u:-?},mutual=${m:-?})"
done
[ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || echo "iSCSI adapters without bidirectional CHAP:$bad"

remediation.command: To enable bidirectional CHAP authentication for iSCSI traffic, perform the following: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure then expand Storage. 3. Select Storage Adapters then select the iSCSI Adapter. 4. Under Properties click on Edit next to Authentication. 5. Next to Authentication Method select Use bidirectional CHAP from the dropdown. 6. Specify the outgoing CHAP name. Make sure that the name you specify matches the name configured on the storage side. To set the CHAP name to the iSCSI adapter name, select "Use initiator name".

title: Host iSCSI client, if enabled, must employ unique CHAP authentication secrets
description: Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol (CHAP) requires both client and host to know a secret to establish a connection. It is essential to employ unique CHAP authentication secrets for each iSCSI session to ensure secure communications. The parameter governing this behavior is outlined in the iSCSI or iSER storage adapter configuration under CHAP settings. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 6.3.2 Host iSCSI client, if enabled, must employ unique CHAP authentication secrets

audit.command: To verify the CHAP secrets are unique, run the following to list all iSCSI adapters and their corresponding CHAP configuration: # List Iscsi Initiator and CHAP Name if defined Get-VMHost | Get-VMHostHba | Where {$_.Type -eq "Iscsi"} | Select VMHost, Device, ChapType, @{N="CHAPName";E={$_.AuthenticationProperties.ChapName}}

remediation.command: To change the values of CHAP secrets so they are unique, perform the following: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure then expand Storage. 3. Select Storage Adapters then select the iSCSI Adapter. 4. Under Properties click on Edit next to Authentication. 5. Next to Authentication Method specify the authentication method from the dropdown. None Use unidirectional CHAP if required by target Use unidirectional CHAP unless prohibited by target Use unidirectional CHAP Use bidirectional CHAP 6. Specify the outgoing CHAP name. Make sure that the name you specify matches the name configured on the storage side.

title: Host SNMP services, if enabled, must limit access
description: To manage hosts securely, if SNMP is enabled, access must be restricted. Preferably, SNMPv3 should be employed as it offers superior security through key authentication and encryption compared to SNMPv1 or SNMPv2. Configuring the destination for SNMP traps is essential for ensuring monitoring data is directed to a legitimate and secure host. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 6.4.1 Host SNMP services, if enabled, must limit access

audit.command: To confirm the proper configuration of SNMP, perform the following from the ESXi Shell or vCLI: 1. Run the following to determine if SNMP is being used: esxcli system snmp get 2. If SNMP is being used, refer to the vSphere Monitoring and Performance guide, chapter 8 for steps to verify the parameters. Additionally, the following PowerCLI command may be used to view the SNMP configuration: # List the SNMP Configuration of a host (single host connection required) Get-VMHostSnmp

remediation.command: To correct the SNMP configuration, perform the following from the ESXi Shell or vCLI: 1. If SNMP is not needed, disable it by running: esxcli system snmp set --enable false 2. If SNMP is needed, refer to the vSphere Monitoring and Performance guide, chapter 8 for steps to configure it. Additionally, the following PowerCLI command may be used to implement the configuration: # Update the host SNMP Configuration (single host connection required) Get-VmHostSNMP | Set-VMHostSNMP -Enabled:$true -ReadOnlyCommunity '<secret>' Notes: SNMP must be configured on each ESXi host SNMP settings can be configured using Host Profiles

title: Host SSH daemon, if enabled, must use FIPS 140-2/140-3 validated ciphers
description: For enhanced security, if the SSH daemon is enabled on the host, it must utilize FIPS 140-2/140-3 validated ciphers. This requirement ensures the encryption standards are robust and compliant with regulatory mandates. The audit reads the Ciphers directive of /etc/ssh/sshd_config and requires only AES-based (FIPS-approved) ciphers. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 6.5.1 Host SSH daemon, if enabled, must use FIPS 140-2/140-3 validated ciphers

audit.command:
f=/etc/ssh/sshd_config; [ -r "$f" ] || exit 1
c=$(awk 'tolower($1)=="ciphers" {print tolower($2); exit}' "$f")
[ -n "$c" ] || { echo 'Ciphers not set explicitly'; exit 1; }
bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$c" | tr ',' '\n' | grep -v '^aes' | tr '\n' ' ')
[ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || echo "non-FIPS ciphers: $bad"

remediation.guidance: To remediate this recommendation, configure the SSH daemon to use only the approved FIPS-capable cipher list supported by the installed ESXi build. Validate access from approved administration clients before deploying broadly.

title: Host SSH daemon, if enabled, must use FIPS 140-2/140-3 validated cryptographic modules
description: When enabled, the SSH daemon on the host should employ FIPS 140-2/140-3 validated cryptographic modules provided by OpenSSH. Although these modules are enabled by default, they can be deactivated for backward compatibility, thus auditing and ensuring the correct setting is crucial for maintaining security standards. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 6.5.2 Host SSH daemon, if enabled, must use FIPS 140-2/140-3 validated cryptographic modules

audit.command: Verify ESXi is operating with Broadcom-supported cryptographic modules and that SSH is using the platform-provided OpenSSH/crypto libraries. Review installed VIBs and do not accept replacement third-party SSH/crypto binaries.

remediation.command: To remediate this recommendation, remove unsupported SSH/cryptographic binaries and restore the signed ESXi components from an approved image/profile. Keep ESXi patched so the validated cryptographic modules remain current.

title: Host SSH daemon, if enabled, must not allow use of gateway ports
description: When enabled, the SSH daemon on the host should have the gateway ports feature disabled to prevent remote hosts from forwarding connections. This is a hardening measure to ensure that the SSH service is securely configured against potential forwarding misuses. The audit reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config and requires GatewayPorts no (unset = OpenSSH default no). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 6.5.3 Host SSH daemon, if enabled, must not allow use of gateway ports

audit.command:
f=/etc/ssh/sshd_config; [ -r "$f" ] || exit 1
v=$(awk 'tolower($1)=="gatewayports" {print tolower($2); exit}' "$f")
case "$v" in '') echo compliant ;; no) echo compliant ;; *) echo "GatewayPorts $v" ;; esac

remediation.guidance: To remediate this recommendation, set GatewayPorts no in the supported ESXi SSH configuration. Restart SSH only during an authorized maintenance/admin window and verify the effective setting.

title: Host SSH daemon, if enabled, must not allow host-based authentication
description: Ensuring the SSH daemon on the host disallows host-based authentication is a crucial step towards hardening system services. This prevents a host from authenticating on behalf of the users, thereby enforcing individual accountability and minimizing the risk of unauthorized access. The audit reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config and requires HostbasedAuthentication no (unset = OpenSSH default no). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 6.5.4 Host SSH daemon, if enabled, must not allow host-based authentication

audit.command:
f=/etc/ssh/sshd_config; [ -r "$f" ] || exit 1
v=$(awk 'tolower($1)=="hostbasedauthentication" {print tolower($2); exit}' "$f")
case "$v" in '') echo compliant ;; no) echo compliant ;; *) echo "HostbasedAuthentication $v" ;; esac

remediation.guidance: To remediate this recommendation, set HostbasedAuthentication no, restart SSH if it is authorized to run, and verify host-based authentication is rejected.

title: Host SSH daemon, if enabled, must set a timeout count on idle sessions
description: Setting a timeout count on idle SSH sessions ensures that inactive sessions are automatically disconnected after a specified period. This period is calculated by multiplying the timeout count with the idle timeout interval. Automatic disconnection of idle sessions reduces the window of opportunity for unauthorized access. The audit reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config and requires ClientAliveCountMax to be set to a non-zero value; confirm it matches the approved value. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 6.5.5 Host SSH daemon, if enabled, must set a timeout count on idle sessions

audit.command:
f=/etc/ssh/sshd_config; [ -r "$f" ] || exit 1
v=$(awk 'tolower($1)=="clientalivecountmax" {print $2; exit}' "$f")
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9]*) echo 'ClientAliveCountMax ${v:-not set}'; exit 1 ;; esac
[ "$v" -gt 0 ] && echo compliant || echo 'ClientAliveCountMax is 0'

remediation.guidance: To remediate this recommendation, set ClientAliveCountMax to the approved value, then restart SSH if enabled and test that inactive sessions are closed after the configured interval/count.

title: Host SSH daemon, if enabled, must set a timeout interval on idle sessions

{ line = $0; sub(/^[ \t]+/, "", line); i = index(line, "="); if (i == 0) next

Click on the VM Options tab then expand Advanced. 3. Click on EDIT CONFIGURATION. 4. Click on ADD CONFIGURATION PARAMS then input log.keepOld with a value of 10. 5. Click OK, then OK again. To set the number of log files to be used to 10, run the following PowerCLI command: # Add the setting to all VMs Get-VM | New-AdvancedSetting -Name "log.keepOld" -value "10"

title: Virtual machines must limit the size of diagnostic logs
description: Limiting the size of diagnostic logs on virtual machines ensures efficient utilization of datastore space, particularly beneficial for long-running VMs. This control assists in maintaining an optimal balance between diagnostic capabilities and storage resources. The parameter governing this behavior is log.rotateSize. Expected: log.rotateSize = "1024000". The audit parses every .vmx file under /vmfs/volumes/ on the host and lists the VMs that do not comply; it passes when none are found (or no VMs exist). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 7.27 Virtual machines must limit the size of diagnostic logs

audit.command:
command -v find >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1
out=$(find /vmfs/volumes/ -maxdepth 3 -type f -name '*.vmx' 2>/dev/null | while IFS= read -r f; do
  awk -v KEYRE='^log[.]rotatesize$' -v MODE='eq' -v VAL='1024000' 'BEGIN { re = tolower(KEYRE) }
{ line = $0; sub(/^[ \t]+/, "", line); i = index(line, "="); if (i == 0) next
  k = tolower(substr(line, 1, i - 1)); sub(/[ \t]+$/, "", k)
  v = substr(line, i + 1); sub(/^[ \t]*"?/, "", v); sub(/"?[ \t\r]*$/, "", v); v = tolower(v)
  if (k ~ re) { seen = 1; if (MODE == "not" && v == tolower(VAL)) bad = bad " " k "=" v
                else if (MODE != "not" && MODE != "ge" && v != tolower(VAL)) bad = bad " " k "=" v
                else if (MODE == "ge" && (v + 0) < (VAL + 0)) bad = bad " " k "=" v } }
END { if ((MODE == "eq" || MODE == "ge") && !seen) bad = " " KEYRE " not set"
      if (bad != "") print FILENAME ":" bad }' "$f"
done)
[ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 25

remediation.guidance: To set this configuration utilize the vSphere interface as follows: 1. Select the VM then select Actions followed by Edit Settings. 2. Click on the VM Options tab then expand Advanced. 3. Click on EDIT CONFIGURATION. 4. Click on ADD CONFIGURATION PARAMS then input log.rotateSize with a value of 1024000. 5. Click OK, then OK again. To properly limit the maximum log file size, run the following PowerCLI command: # Add the setting to all VMs Get-VM | New-AdvancedSetting -Name "log.rotateSize" -value "1024000"

title: Virtual machines must limit informational messages from the virtual machine to the VMX file
description: Limit the number of informational messages from the virtual machine to the VMX file to prevent the file from exceeding its default size of 1MB, thereby avoiding potential denial of service situations due to a full datastore. The parameter governing this behavior is tools.setInfo.sizeLimit with a recommended setting of 1048576 or Undefined. Expected: tools.setInfo.sizeLimit set to a finite value. The audit parses every .vmx file under /vmfs/volumes/ on the host and lists the VMs that do not comply; it passes when none are found (or no VMs exist). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 7.28 Virtual machines must limit informational messages from the virtual machine to the VMX file

audit.command:
command -v find >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1
out=$(find /vmfs/volumes/ -maxdepth 3 -type f -name '*.vmx' 2>/dev/null | while IFS= read -r f; do
  awk -v KEYRE='^tools[.]setinfo[.]sizelimit$' -v MODE='ge' -v VAL='1' 'BEGIN { re = tolower(KEYRE) }
{ line = $0; sub(/^[ \t]+/, "", line); i = index(line, "="); if (i == 0) next
  k = tolower(substr(line, 1, i - 1)); sub(/[ \t]+$/, "", k)
  v = substr(line, i + 1); sub(/^[ \t]*"?/, "", v); sub(/"?[ \t\r]*$/, "", v); v = tolower(v)
  if (k ~ re) { seen = 1; if (MODE == "not" && v == tolower(VAL)) bad = bad " " k "=" v
                else if (MODE != "not" && MODE != "ge" && v != tolower(VAL)) bad = bad " " k "=" v
                else if (MODE == "ge" && (v + 0) < (VAL + 0)) bad = bad " " k "=" v } }
END { if ((MODE == "eq" || MODE == "ge") && !seen) bad = " " KEYRE " not set"
      if (bad != "") print FILENAME ":" bad }' "$f"
done)
[ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 25

remediation.guidance: To remediate this recommendation, set tools.setInfo.sizeLimit to the organization-approved limit using Set-AdvancedSetting/New-AdvancedSetting. Validate any guest-management tooling that relies on guest information exchange.

title: VMware Tools must be a version that has not reached End of General Support status
description: Ensuring VMware Tools is running a version that has not reached its End of General Support (EOGS) status is imperative for maintaining a secure and supported environment. A version within its support period guarantees regular updates, security patches, and vendor support. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 8.1 VMware Tools must be a version that has not reached End of General Support status

audit.command: Inside each guest OS: Within each applicable guest operating system, execute VMwareToolboxCmd.exe - v. Compare the installed VMware Tools version to Broadcom lifecycle/support information and verify it has not reached End of General Support.

remediation.command: To remediate this recommendation, upgrade VMware Tools to a supported release using vSphere, the guest package manager/open-vm-tools, or an enterprise software deployment tool. Reboot the guest if required and verify the installed version.

title: VMware Tools must have all software updates installed
description: Ensuring that all software updates are installed on VMware Tools is crucial for maintaining a healthy and secure virtual environment. These updates provide essential drivers, enable effective management of guest operating systems, and offer features necessary for VM deployment and customization. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 8.2 VMware Tools must have all software updates installed

audit.command: Inside each guest OS: Determine the installed VMware Tools version in each guest and compare it with the current approved security/update baseline. Review Broadcom security advisories for fixes applicable to that Tools release.

remediation.command: To remediate this recommendation, install all approved VMware Tools updates using vSphere, open-vm-tools packages, or enterprise endpoint management. Reboot if required and verify the post-update version.

title: VMware Tools should configure automatic upgrades as appropriate for the environment
description: Automatic upgrades of VMware Tools can be managed via vSphere, ensuring VMware Tools versions remain current. This functionality is advisable unless alternative management and update mechanisms are in place. It is recommended to have automatic updates enabled to minimize administrative overhead and maintain up-to- date features and security patches. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 8.3 VMware Tools should configure automatic upgrades as appropriate for the environment

audit.command: Inside each guest OS: Review each VM's VMware Tools upgrade policy in vSphere (Edit Settings > VM Options > VMware Tools) and the guest's package-management policy. Verify that automatic upgrade behavior matches the organization's approved change-management model.

remediation.command: To remediate this recommendation, enable automatic VMware Tools upgrades only where appropriate, or configure a controlled centralized update process. In vSphere select the approved 'check and upgrade Tools during power cycling' behavior as appropriate for the environment.

title: VMware Tools must limit the automatic addition of features
description: Limit the automatic addition of features during VMware Tools upgrade processes to maintain the desired security profile of the guest operating system from vSphere. This control can be managed by setting the configuration parameter to a specified value. The parameter governing this behavior is autoupgrade allow-add-feature with a recommended setting of false. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 8.5 VMware Tools must limit the automatic addition of features

audit.command: Inside each guest OS: Review VMware Tools configuration for automatic feature installation. Verify that automatic addition of optional Tools features is disabled or restricted unless explicitly required by the guest's management design.

remediation.command: To remediate this recommendation, configure VMware Tools so optional features are not automatically added during reconfiguration/upgrade. Use the supported vmware- toolbox-cmd config set/Windows VMwareToolboxCmd.exe config set mechanism or enterprise deployment package and document required exceptions.

title: VMware Tools must limit the automatic removal of features
description: Limiting the automatic removal of features by VMware Tools during upgrade processes is crucial to maintain the intended security profile of the guest OS from vSphere. The automatic upgrade could potentially remove essential features, impacting the security posture inadvertently. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 8.6 VMware Tools must limit the automatic removal of features

audit.command: Inside each guest OS: Review VMware Tools configuration for automatic feature removal. Verify that features are not automatically removed unless the behavior is explicitly approved.

remediation.command: To remediate this recommendation, configure VMware Tools to prevent automatic removal of installed features during reconfiguration/upgrade unless required. Apply the guest-OS-specific VMware Tools configuration and validate application dependencies.

title: VMware Tools must deactivate GlobalConf unless required
description: The GlobalConf feature within VMware Tools facilitates the delivery of tools.conf configurations to virtual machines, simplifying configuration management. However, if not necessary, it's advisable to deactivate this feature to reduce potential security risks. The parameter governing this behavior is globalconf enabled with a recommended setting of false. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 8.7 VMware Tools must deactivate GlobalConf unless required

audit.command: Inside each guest OS: Within the guest operating system 1. Execute `VMwareToolboxCmd.exe config get globalconf enabled```. Unless required, verify the value is false.

remediation.command: To remediate this recommendation, execute VMwareToolboxCmd.exe equivalent. Restart VMware Tools if required and verify the setting.

title: VMware Tools must deactivate Guest Store Upgrade operations unless required
description: The GuestStore feature facilitates the distribution of specific content to multiple guests. If not required, it is advisable to disable this plugin to minimize potential attack vectors. The parameter governing this behavior is gueststoreupgrade policy with a recommended setting of off. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 8.10 VMware Tools must deactivate Guest Store Upgrade operations unless required

audit.command: Inside each guest OS: Within the guest operating system, execute vmware-toolbox-cmd config get gueststoreupgrade policy (or VMwareToolboxCmd.exe). Unless required, verify the value is off.

remediation.command: To remediate this recommendation, execute vmware-toolbox-cmd config set gueststoreupgrade policy off or the Windows equivalent. Restart VMware Tools if required and verify the setting.

title: VMware Tools must limit the use of MSI transforms when reconfiguring VMware Tools
description: Limiting the use of MSI transforms during VMware Tools reconfiguration is crucial to prevent unintended alterations to the installation database on Microsoft Windows guest operating systems from vSphere. This control is managed through a specific configuration parameter. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 8.12 VMware Tools must limit the use of MSI transforms when reconfiguring VMware Tools

audit.command: Inside each guest OS: On applicable Windows guests, execute VMwareToolboxCmd.exe config get autoupgrade allow-msi-transforms. Verify that the value is false. Treat this control as not applicable to non-Windows guests that do not use MSI.

remediation.command: To remediate this recommendation, execute VMwareToolboxCmd.exe config set autoupgrade allow-msi-transforms false. Restart VMware Tools if required and verify the value remains false.

title: VMware Tools must enable VMware Tools logging
description: Enable logging within VMware Tools to ensure the collection of pertinent information, facilitating diagnostic or forensic activities. Logging within VMware Tools is highly customizable, allowing for tailored logging setups. The parameter governing this behavior is logging log with a recommended setting of true. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 8.13 VMware Tools must enable VMware Tools logging

audit.command: Inside each guest OS: Review VMware Tools logging configuration inside the guest using vmware-toolbox-cmd config get logging log / the applicable tools.conf settings. Verify that Tools logging is enabled and produces expected log records.

remediation.command: Enable VMware Tools logging using the guest's supported tools.conf/vmware-toolbox- cmd config set mechanism. Restart the VMware Tools service if required and verify log generation.

title: VMware Tools must send VMware Tools logs to the system log service
description: Adjusting the logging destination in VMware Tools from the default file on disk to system log services streamlines log management. It redirects logs to syslog on Linux guests and the Windows Event Service on Microsoft Windows guests for centralized monitoring, management, and archiving. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 9.0 Benchmark v1.0.0 - 8.14 VMware Tools must send VMware Tools logs to the system log service

audit.command: Inside each guest OS: Review VMware Tools logging destination and verify Tools messages are sent to the guest operating system's system logging facility (syslog/journald on Linux or the approved Windows logging mechanism) rather than only to an unmanaged local file.

remediation.command: To remediate this recommendation, configure VMware Tools logging to use the system log service for the guest OS. Restart VMware Tools if required and verify a test Tools event reaches the system log.

title: Host hardware must have auditable, authentic, and up to date system & device firmware
description: Hardware firmware is not immune to serious issues affecting confidentiality, integrity, or availability. Vulnerable system management controllers & management engines can provide places for attackers to establish persistence, in order to re-infect and re- compromise hosts after reboots and updates. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 1.1 Host hardware must have auditable, authentic, and up to date system & device firmware

audit.command: The preferred approach is to utilize a vendor-supported, VMware-compatible firmware and driver combination. Leverage Broadcom's Lifecycle Manager hardware compatibility checks or similar tools if available. If that is not available, manually inventory: ; System BIOS/UEFI ; BMC / iDRAC / iLO firmware ; TPM firmware ; RAID/storage controller firmware ; HBA firmware ; NIC firmware ; Fibre Channel adapter firmware ; NVMe / storage-device firmware where applicable

remediation.command: Proposed remediation guidelines: 1. Verify the exact server model and hardware components. 2. Obtain firmware only from the OEM/vendor: o Dell o HPE o Lenovo o Cisco o etc. 3. Verify that the proposed firmware and associated ESXi driver are supported for your ESXi 8 release. 4. Place the ESXi host in maintenance mode. 5. Apply firmware through the vendor-supported mechanism (for example): o Dell iDRAC / OpenManage o HPE iLO / SPP o Lenovo XClarity o Cisco UCS Manager o Vendor bootable firmware package o Vendor Hardware Support Manager 6. Reboot the physical host if required. 7. Re-run the firmware inventory. 8. Confirm device/driver/firmware compatibility. 9. Exit maintenance mode.

title: Host hardware must enable Intel TXT, if available
description: Intel Xeon Scalable Processor platforms have Trusted Execution Technology, or TXT, that help harden systems against malware, rootkits, BIOS & firmware attacks, and more. When enabled, ESXi will take advantage of security benefits offered by this technology. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 1.3 Host hardware must enable Intel TXT, if available

audit.command: 1. Execute: esxcli hardware trustedboot get 2. For hardware that supports Intel Trusted Execution Technology, verify: Drtm Enabled: true Tpm Present: true Note: If Drtm Enabled is false, determine whether Intel TXT is supported by the host hardware and firmware. If TXT is supported but not enabled, the host is not compliant.

remediation.command: Place the ESXi host into maintenance mode and reboot the physical server. Enter the system BIOS/UEFI configuration and enable TPM 2.0 and Intel Trusted Execution Technology (TXT), where supported. Save the firmware configuration and perform a full reboot.

title: Host hardware must enable and configure a TPM 2.0
description: ESXi can use Trusted Platform Modules (TPM) 2.0 to enable advanced security features that prevent malware, remove dependencies, and secure hardware lifecycle operations. The audit runs esxcli hardware trustedboot get and requires "Tpm Present: true"; TPM attestation alarms are still reviewed in vCenter. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 1.4 Host hardware must enable and configure a TPM 2.0

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli hardware trustedboot get 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk -F': *' 'tolower($1) ~ /^ *tpm present$/ {print $2; exit}' | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | sed 's/ *$//')
if [ "$v" = true ]; then echo compliant; else echo "Tpm Present: ${v:-not reported}"; fi

remediation.command: 1. Place the host in maintenance mode. 2. reboot into BIOS/UEFI. 3. Enable and activate the TPM 4. Select TPM 2.0 mode, and ensure UEFI/Secure Boot prerequisites required by the server vendor are enabled. 5. Save changes. 6. reboot with command reboot 7. Verify again with esxcli hardware trustedboot get and esxcli system settings encryption get.

title: Host integrated hardware management controller must be secure
description: Many servers have integrated hardware management controllers that can be extremely helpful when monitoring and updating hardware, settings, and firmware. These controllers should be checked to ensure that ALL unused functionality is disabled, ALL unused access methods are disabled, passwords and password controls are set, and firewalling and access control is in place so that ... Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 1.5 Host integrated hardware management controller must be secure

audit.command: 1. Verify whether the ESXi host exposes a BMC interface: esxcli hardware ipmi bmc get 2. Find the hardware management controller and review: ; Firmware is current and vendor-supported. ; Default accounts and default passwords are not in use. ; Administrative accounts are individually assigned. ; Strong password/authentication policy is configured. ; MFA is enabled where supported. ; HTTPS/TLS is used for web management. ; Weak or obsolete protocols are disabled. ; SSH/IPMI access is disabled unless operationally required. ; Management access is restricted to authorized management networks.

remediation.command: Configure the controller according to the organization's secure-management baseline.

title: Host integrated hardware management controller must enable time synchronization
description: Cryptography, audit logging, cluster operations, and incident response/forensics depend deeply on synchronized time. This recommendation extends to all devices in infrastructure. The recommendation for NTP is to have at least four sources. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 1.6 Host integrated hardware management controller must enable time synchronization

audit.command: 1. Verify that NTP or another approved time synchronization mechanism is enabled 2. Verify that the ESXi host uses reliable time synchronization esxcli system ntp get

remediation.command: 1. Enable NTP or the vendor-supported automatic time synchronization service. 2. Enter the organization's approved NTP servers. 3. Configure multiple authoritative NTP sources where supported. 4. Configure the appropriate time zone. 5. Save/apply the configuration.

title: Host integrated hardware management controller must enable remote logging of events
description: The host's integrated hardware management controller provides critical out-of-band server oversight. For enhanced security, it is essential to configure this controller to log events remotely. This practice ensures that hardware-related logs are sent to an off-site location, protecting them from potential tampering and offering a centralized record of server health and ... Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 1.7 Host integrated hardware management controller must enable remote logging of events

audit.command: Access the hardware management controller and verify that remote event logging/syslog forwarding is enabled and configured to send hardware, security, authentication, and management events to an approved centralized log collector.

remediation.command: Locate the controller's Syslog, Remote Logging, Event Forwarding, or equivalent configuration and: 1. Enable remote event logging. 2. Configure the hostname or IP address of the approved centralized log collector. 3. Configure the appropriate port and protocol. 4. Use TLS or another protected transport where supported. 5. Select the required event categories, including hardware, security, authentication, firmware, and administrative events. 6. Save the configuration.

title: Host must run software that has not reached End of General Support status
description: The "End of General Support" (EOGS) status indicates that the software version has exceeded its primary support lifecycle, during which VMware provides new security patches, bug fixes, and technical assistance. When a product reaches this status, VMware no longer releases security updates for that version for customers outside of an extended support contract. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 2.1 Host must run software that has not reached End of General Support status

audit.command: 1. Execute vmware -vl or esxcli system version get 2. Record the ESXi version/build. 3. Compare the installed release to Broadcom's current lifecycle/support matrix. The host is compliant only when the installed ESXi release remains within General Support.

remediation.command: To remediate this recommendation, upgrade the host to an ESXi release/build that is still within Broadcom General Support. Use vSphere Lifecycle Manager or the vendor- supported image, validate hardware compatibility first, place the host in maintenance mode, remediate/upgrade, reboot, and verify the new build.

title: Host must have all software updates installed
description: Applying updates in a timely manner according to the severity of issues contributes greatly to the resilience of an environment. When applying updates, it is recommended to update vCenter Server first, if an update is available, and then proceed with updating ESXi. This sequence ensures that the management layer is updated before updating the ESXi hosts. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 2.2 Host must have all software updates installed

audit.command: Verify that the patches are up to date. The following PowerCLI snippet will provide a list of all installed patches: Foreach ($VMHost in Get-VMHost ) { $EsxCli = Get-EsxCli -VMHost $VMHost -V2 $EsxCli.software.vib.list.invoke() | Select-Object @{N="VMHost";E={$VMHost}},* } You may also manage updates via VMware Lifecycle Manager located under Menu, Lifecycle Manager.

remediation.command: Use VMware Lifecycle Manager to update and upgrade hosts when ESXi is managed through VMware vCenter. For standalone hosts use esxcli or API-driven methods for applying updates. Employ a process to keep ESXi hosts up to date with patches in accordance with industry standards and internal guidelines. Leverage the VMware Lifecycle Manager to test and apply patches as they become available.

title: Host must enable Secure Boot enforcement
description: Enabling Secure Boot enforcement ensures that the host only loads UEFI drivers and applications with valid digital signatures, as part of the UEFI firmware standard. It requires support from the server's BIOS and hypervisor boot loader, and mandates that all ESXi kernel modules, drivers, and VIBs be signed by VMware or a trusted partner subordinate. The audit runs esxcli system settings encryption get and requires "Require Secure Boot: true". Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 2.3 Host must enable Secure Boot enforcement

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings encryption get 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk -F': *' 'tolower($1) ~ /^ *require secure boot$/ {print $2; exit}' | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | sed 's/ *$//')
if [ "$v" = true ]; then echo compliant; else echo "Require Secure Boot: ${v:-not reported}"; fi

remediation.command: 1. Enable UEFI Secure Boot and TPM 2.0 on the hardware. 2. Configure ESXi secure configuration/Secure Boot enforcement using the supported vSphere/ESXCLI procedure for the installed ESXi 8 build. 3. Reboot if required and verify both secureBoot.py -s and esxcli system settings encryption get

title: Host must only run binaries delivered via signed VIB
description: The ESXi host is configured to only execute binaries originating from a valid, signed vSphere Installable Bundle (VIB) to enhance the integrity of the system. This measure thwarts attackers' attempts to use prebuilt toolkits on the host. The parameter governing this behavior is VMkernel.Boot.execInstalledOnly with a recommended setting of True. The audit runs esxcli system settings kernel list -o execInstalledOnly and requires the configured and runtime values to be TRUE. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 2.5 Host must only run binaries delivered via signed VIB

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings kernel list -o execInstalledOnly 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
set -- $(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="execInstalledOnly" {print toupper($3), toupper($4); exit}')
[ $# -eq 0 ] && { echo 'execInstalledOnly not listed'; exit 1; }
[ "$1" = TRUE ] && [ "$2" = TRUE ] && echo compliant || echo "execInstalledOnly configured=$1 runtime=$2"

remediation.guidance: 1. Remove unauthorized VIBs and set the kernel option with esxcli system settings kernel set -s execInstalledOnly -v TRUE 2. Reboot if the command or build indicates a reboot is required 3. Re-run the audit command and confirm only approved signed VIB-delivered binaries are executable.

title: Host must have reliable time synchronization sources
description: Ensuring reliable time synchronization is crucial as various functions like cryptography, audit logging, cluster operations, and incident response/forensics are heavily dependent on synchronized time. Utilizing at least four NTP sources is recommended for achieving reliable time synchronization. The audit runs esxcli system ntp get and requires NTP to be enabled with at least one server. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 2.6 Host must have reliable time synchronization sources

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system ntp get 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
en=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/^ *Enabled: *//p' | head -n 1)
srv=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/^ *Servers\{0,1\}: *//p' | head -n 1)
[ "$en" = true ] && [ -n "$srv" ] && echo compliant || echo "ntp enabled=$en servers=$srv"

remediation.command: To enable and properly configure NTP synchronization, perform the following from the vSphere web client: 1. Select a host 2. Click Configure then expand System then select Time Configuration. 3. Select Edit next to Network Time Protocol 4. Select the Enable box, then fill in the appropriate NTP Servers. 5. in the NTP Service Startup Policy drop down select Start and stop with host. 6. Click OK.

title: Host must have time synchronization services enabled and running
description: Ensure the host has time synchronization services enabled and operational as many functions such as cryptography, audit logging, cluster operations, and incident response/forensics depend on synchronized time. Services like NTP or PTP should be configured to start with the host and remain running to maintain time synchronization. The audit requires NTP enabled with servers (esxcli system ntp get) and the ntpd service running (/etc/init.d/ntpd status). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 2.7 Host must have time synchronization services enabled and running

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system ntp get 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
en=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/^ *Enabled: *//p' | head -n 1)
srv=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/^ *Servers\{0,1\}: *//p' | head -n 1)
[ "$en" = true ] && [ -n "$srv" ] || { echo "ntp enabled=$en servers=$srv"; exit 1; }
st=$(/etc/init.d/ntpd status 2>&1)
case "$st" in *'not running'*) echo 'ntpd is not running' ;; *running*) echo compliant ;; *) echo "ntpd status: $st" ;; esac

remediation.command: 1. Configure approved NTP servers 2. Enable the NTP client firewall ruleset if required 3. Set the NTP service startup policy to start and stop with the host, and start the service. Example: esxcli system ntp set --enabled true after configuring approved servers. Verify synchronization after remediation.

title: Host must require TPM-based configuration encryption
description: The host should enforce TPM-based configuration encryption to secure its configuration files, notably within the /etc/ directory or other namespaces. From vSphere 7.0 Update 2 onwards, configuration files archived are encrypted, leveraging a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to "seal" the configuration to the host, thereby enhancing security against offline attacks. The audit runs esxcli system settings encryption get and requires "Mode: TPM". Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 2.8 Host must require TPM-based configuration encryption

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings encryption get 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk -F': *' 'tolower($1) ~ /^ *mode$/ {print $2; exit}' | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | sed 's/ *$//')
if [ "$v" = tpm ]; then echo compliant; else echo "Mode: ${v:-not reported}"; fi

remediation.command: 1. Ensure TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot are enabled. 2. Take a backup of the ESXi recovery key 3. Configure the host to use TPM-backed configuration encryption using the supported ESXi secure-configuration procedure. 4. Reboot if required with the reboot command 5. Re-run esxcli system settings encryption get

title: Host must not suppress warnings about unmitigated hyperthreading vulnerabilities
description: It is imperative to retain hyperthreading security warnings as they indicate unmitigated CPU vulnerabilities. The parameter governing this behavior is UserVars.SuppressHyperthreadWarning, with a recommended setting of 0. The audit reads UserVars.SuppressHyperthreadWarning with esxcli and requires 0. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 2.9 Host must not suppress warnings about unmitigated hyperthreading vulnerabilities

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /UserVars/SuppressHyperthreadWarning 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/UserVars/SuppressHyperthreadWarning: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -eq 0 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/UserVars/SuppressHyperthreadWarning = $v (expected 0)"; fi

remediation.guidance: 1. Utilize the administrative PowerCLI session: execute Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name UserVars.SuppressHyperthreadWarning | Set-AdvancedSetting -Value 0 -Confirm:$false

title: Host must restrict inter-VM transparent page sharing
description: Transparent Page Sharing (TPS) aids in optimizing memory usage among virtual machines but under certain circumstances can be exploited to access data on adjacent virtual machines unauthorizedly. By configuring the Mem.ShareForceSalting parameter, inter-VM TPS is restricted, enhancing isolation and security. The audit reads Mem.ShareForceSalting with esxcli and requires 2. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 2.10 Host must restrict inter-VM transparent page sharing

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Mem/ShareForceSalting 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/Mem/ShareForceSalting: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -eq 2 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Mem/ShareForceSalting = $v (expected 2)"; fi

remediation.guidance: From the vSphere Web Client: 1. Select a host 2. Click Configure then expand System then select Advanced System settings. 3. Click Edit then Filter for Mem.ShareForceSalting. 4. Set the value to 2. 5. Click OK. Additionally, the following PowerCLI command can be used: Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name Mem.ShareForceSalting | Set- AdvancedSetting -Value 2

title: Host must use sufficient entropy for cryptographic operations
description: Starting with vSphere 8.0, ESXi has enhanced its entropy implementation to align with FIPS 140-3 and EAL4 certifications, ensuring a robust foundation for cryptographic operations. Kernel boot options dictate the activation of entropy sources on an ESXi host. The parameter governing this behavior is disableHwrng = FALSE and entropySources = 0. The audit runs esxcli system settings kernel list -o disableHwrng and requires it to be absent or FALSE (configured and runtime). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 2.11 Host must use sufficient entropy for cryptographic operations

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings kernel list -o disableHwrng 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
set -- $(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="disableHwrng" {print toupper($3), toupper($4); exit}')
[ $# -eq 0 ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }
[ "$1" = FALSE ] && [ "$2" = FALSE ] && echo compliant || echo "disableHwrng configured=$1 runtime=$2"

remediation.guidance: 1. Set the kernel option with: esxcli system settings kernel set -s disableHwrng -v FALSE 2. Reboot if required by the host/build and verify the configured and runtime values are FALSE.

title: Host must deactivate SLP
description: The Service Location Protocol (SLP) is used for the discovery and selection of network services in local area networks, which simplifies configuration by allowing computers to find necessary services automatically. The practice of deactivating SLP when not in use aligns with the principle of minimizing the attack surface by shutting down non-essential services. The audit runs /etc/init.d/slpd status and requires "not running". Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 3.4 Host must deactivate SLP

audit.command:
st=$(/etc/init.d/slpd status 2>&1)
case "$st" in *'not running'*) echo compliant ;; *running*) echo 'slpd is running' ;; *) echo "slpd status: $st"; exit 1 ;; esac

remediation.guidance: 1. Stop SLP if running: /etc/init.d/slpd stop Note: Confirm no operational dependency requires SLP before disabling it.

title: Host must deactivate CIM
description: Deactivating the Common Information Model (CIM) service, when not in use, aligns with the principle of minimizing the attack surface by disabling non-essential services. This action helps in reducing the potential vectors of attack, thus bolstering the host's security posture. The audit runs esxcli system wbem get and requires "Enabled: false". Document an exception when CIM is required. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 3.5 Host must deactivate CIM

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system wbem get 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk -F': *' 'tolower($1) ~ /^ *enabled$/ {print $2; exit}' | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | sed 's/ *$//')
if [ "$v" = false ]; then echo compliant; else echo "WBEM Enabled: ${v:-not reported}"; fi

remediation.guidance: Prerequisite Confirm monitoring/storage integrations do not require CIM/WBEM. If not required: 1. Disable WBEM/CIM using: esxcli system wbem set --enable false

title: Host should deactivate SNMP
description: Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) facilitates the management of networked devices. Minimize attack surface by disabling non-essential services. The recommended setting is to have the SNMP service stopped unless required and configured securely. The audit runs esxcli system snmp get and requires "Enable: false". When SNMP is required, document the exception and apply 6.4.1. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 3.6 Host should deactivate SNMP

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system snmp get 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk -F': *' 'tolower($1) ~ /^ *enable$/ {print $2; exit}' | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | sed 's/ *$//')
if [ "$v" = false ]; then echo compliant; else echo "SNMP Enable: ${v:-not reported}"; fi

remediation.guidance: 1. Disable SNMP when not required with: esxcli system snmp set --enable false If SNMP is required, restrict targets/communities, prefer secure SNMP configurations supported by the environment, and limit the ESXi firewall ruleset to authorized management networks.

title: Host must automatically terminate idle DCUI sessions
description: By configuring a session timeout, unattended console sessions are automatically terminated, thereby reducing the potential security risks associated with lingering active sessions. The parameter governing this behavior is UserVars.DcuiTimeOut, with a recommended setting of 600 (10 minutes). The audit reads UserVars.DcuiTimeOut with esxcli and requires 600 seconds or less (0 disables the timeout and fails). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 3.7 Host must automatically terminate idle DCUI sessions

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /UserVars/DcuiTimeOut 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/UserVars/DcuiTimeOut: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -gt 0 ] && [ "$v" -le 600 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/UserVars/DcuiTimeOut = $v (expected 1-600)"; fi

remediation.guidance: To correct the DCUI timeout setting, perform the following steps: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure, then under System select Advanced System Settings. 3. Select Edit then enter UserVars.DcuiTimeOut in the filter. 4. Click in the box for the current value, then set the value to 600 seconds or less. Alternately, use the following PowerCLI command: Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name UserVars.DcuiTimeOut | Set- AdvancedSetting -Value 600

title: Host must automatically terminate idle shells
description: The host should be configured to automatically terminate idle shell sessions to prevent potential unauthorized access due to forgotten logouts. Setting a timeout for idle SSH connections ensures that any unattended sessions are closed, thereby reducing the security risk. The parameter governing this behavior is UserVars. The audit reads UserVars.ESXiShellInteractiveTimeOut with esxcli and requires 300 seconds or less (0 disables it and fails). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 3.8 Host must automatically terminate idle shells

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /UserVars/ESXiShellInteractiveTimeOut 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/UserVars/ESXiShellInteractiveTimeOut: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -gt 0 ] && [ "$v" -le 300 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/UserVars/ESXiShellInteractiveTimeOut = $v (expected 1-300)"; fi

remediation.guidance: To set the timeout to the desired value, perform the following from the vSphere web client: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure then expand System. 3. Select Advanced System Settings then click Edit. 4. Enter ESXiShellInteractiveTimeOut in the filter. 5. Set the value for this parameter is set to the appropriate value (300 seconds or less). 6. Click OK. Note: A value of 0 disables the ESXi ShellInteractiveTimeOut. Alternately, use the following PowerCLI command: # Set Remove UserVars.ESXiShellInteractiveTimeOut to 300 on all hosts Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name 'UserVars.ESXiShellInteractiveTimeOut' | Set-AdvancedSetting -Value "300"

title: Host must automatically deactivate shell services
description: Enabling the automatic deactivation of shell services minimizes the attack surface on the host. The time window for the ESXi Shell and SSH services' availability is defined by UserVars.ESXiShellTimeOut, after which these services are terminated. The recommended setting for this parameter is 3600. The audit reads UserVars.ESXiShellTimeOut with esxcli and requires 3600 seconds or less (0 disables it and fails). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 3.9 Host must automatically deactivate shell services

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /UserVars/ESXiShellTimeOut 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/UserVars/ESXiShellTimeOut: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -gt 0 ] && [ "$v" -le 3600 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/UserVars/ESXiShellTimeOut = $v (expected 1-3600)"; fi

remediation.guidance: To set the timeout to the desired value, perform the following from the vSphere web client: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure then expand System. 3. Select Advanced System Settings then click Edit. 4. Enter ESXiShellTimeOut in the filter. 5. Set the value for this parameter is set to 3600 (1 hour) or less 6. Click OK. Note: A value of 0 disables the ESXiShellTimeOut. Alternately, run the following PowerCLI command: # Set UserVars.ESXiShellTimeOut to 3600 on all hosts Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name 'UserVars.ESXiShellTimeOut' | Set- AdvancedSetting -Value "3600"

title: Host must not suppress warnings that the shell is enabled
description: Having warnings for enabled SSH or ESXi Shell provides insight into potential security risks. Disabling such warnings can mask ongoing attacks. The parameter governing this behavior is UserVars.SuppressShellWarning with a recommended value of 0. The audit reads UserVars.SuppressShellWarning with esxcli and requires 0. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 3.10 Host must not suppress warnings that the shell is enabled

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /UserVars/SuppressShellWarning 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/UserVars/SuppressShellWarning: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -eq 0 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/UserVars/SuppressShellWarning = $v (expected 0)"; fi

remediation.guidance: From an administrative PowerCLI session. 1. Execute Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name UserVars.SuppressShellWarning | Set-AdvancedSetting -Value 0 - Confirm:$false 2. Shell access should normally remain disabled; do not suppress the warning when it is enabled.

title: Host must lock an account after a specified number of failed login attempts
description: The security control involves restricting account access following a specified number of failed login attempts, acting as a deterrent against brute-force attacks. This control is applicable for SSH and vSphere Web Services SDK access, though not for the Direct Console Interface (DCUI) and the ESXi Shell. The audit reads Security.AccountLockFailures with esxcli and requires 5. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 3.12 Host must lock an account after a specified number of failed login attempts

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Security/AccountLockFailures 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/Security/AccountLockFailures: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -eq 5 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Security/AccountLockFailures = $v (expected 5)"; fi

remediation.guidance: To set the maximum failed login attempts correctly, perform the following steps: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure then expand System. 3. Select Advanced System Settings then click Edit. 4. Enter Security.AccountLockFailures in the filter. 5. Set the value for this parameter to 5. Alternately, use the following PowerCLI command: Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name Security.AccountLockFailures | Set- AdvancedSetting -Value 5

title: Host must unlock accounts after a specified timeout period
description: Ensuring that user accounts on the ESXi host are automatically unlocked after a specified period contributes to a balance between security and operational usability. This mechanism reactivates idle accounts promptly while mitigating potential unauthorized access risks. The audit reads Security.AccountUnlockTime with esxcli and requires 900 seconds. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 3.13 Host must unlock accounts after a specified timeout period

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Security/AccountUnlockTime 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/Security/AccountUnlockTime: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -eq 900 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Security/AccountUnlockTime = $v (expected 900)"; fi

remediation.guidance: To set the account lockout to 15 minutes, perform the following: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure then expand System. 3. Select Advanced System Settings then click Edit. 4. Enter Security.AccountUnlockTime in the filter. 5. Set the value for this parameter to 900. Alternately, use the following PowerCLI command: Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name Security.AccountUnlockTime | Set- AdvancedSetting -Value 900

title: Host must configure the password history setting to restrict the reuse of passwords
description: The goal is to inhibit the reuse of past passwords, acting as a deterrent against potential security breaches stemming from the exploitation of old, compromised credentials. This is achieved by configuring the Security.PasswordHistory parameter, which specifies the number of unique passwords a user must cycle through before a previous password can be reused. The audit reads Security.PasswordHistory with esxcli and requires 5. Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 3.14 Host must configure the password history setting to restrict the reuse of passwords

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Security/PasswordHistory 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/Security/PasswordHistory: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -eq 5 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Security/PasswordHistory = $v (expected 5)"; fi

remediation.guidance: To set the password history 5, perform the following: 1. From the vSphere Web Client, select the host. 2. Click Configure then expand System. 3. Select Advanced System Settings then click Edit. 4. Enter Security.PasswordHistory in the filter. 5. Set the value for this parameter is set to 5. Alternately, the following PowerCLI command may be used: Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting Security.PasswordHistory | Set- AdvancedSetting -Value 5

title: Host must be configured with an appropriate maximum password age
description: Implementing a maximum password age, as determined by the Security.PasswordMaxDays parameter, is aligned with modern password policies outlined in NIST 800-63B Section 5.1.1.2, which argue against forced periodic password changes provided that passwords have sufficient complexity. Manual review: the check needs vCenter/PowerCLI, firmware or guest access, or an organization-specific value.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 3.15 Host must be configured with an appropriate maximum password age

audit.command: From an administrative PowerCLI session 1. Execute Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name Security.PasswordMaxDays 2. Verify that the value matches organizational policy or 99999 when periodic password rotation is not required by policy.

remediation.command: 1. Set the approved value with Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name Security.PasswordMaxDays | Set-AdvancedSetting -Value <approved_days> -Confirm:$false 2. Document any policy-driven value that differs from the benchmark baseline.

title: Host must configure a session timeout for the API
description: A designated timeout ensures that sessions are not left open indefinitely, thereby reducing the exposure window for potential security threats. The parameter governing this behavior is Config.HostAgent.vmacore.soap.sessionTimeout with a recommended setting of 30 seconds. The audit reads Config.HostAgent.vmacore.soap.sessionTimeout with esxcli and requires the recommended 30 or less (0 disables the timeout and fails). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 3.16 Host must configure a session timeout for the API

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /Config/HostAgent/vmacore/soap/sessionTimeout 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/Config/HostAgent/vmacore/soap/sessionTimeout: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
if [ "$v" -gt 0 ] && [ "$v" -le 30 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "/Config/HostAgent/vmacore/soap/sessionTimeout = $v (expected 1-30)"; fi

remediation.guidance: 1. Set the approved timeout with: Get-VMHost | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name Config.HostAgent.vmacore.soap.sessionTimeout | Set- AdvancedSetting -Value <seconds> -Confirm:$false 2. Validate administrative integrations after the change.

title: Host must automatically terminate idle host client sessions
description: Configuring the host to automatically terminate idle host client sessions helps mitigate security risks associated with unattended sessions, which could potentially be exploited. The recommended setting for this control is a timeout value of 900. The parameter governing this behavior is UserVars.HostClientSessionTimeout. The audit reads UserVars.HostClientSessionTimeout with esxcli and requires 900 seconds or less (0 = unlimited fails). Runs in the ESXi Shell (busybox sh) as root.
reference: CIS VMware ESXi 8.0 Benchmark v1.4.0 - 3.17 Host must automatically terminate idle host client sessions

audit.command:
out=$(esxcli system settings advanced list -o /UserVars/HostClientSessionTimeout 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$1=="Int" && $2=="Value:" {print $3; exit}')
case "$v" in ''|*[!0-9-]*) echo '/UserVars/HostClientSessionTimeout: no integer value'; exit 1 ;; esac
